div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
Sirs. Will.

Last week's visit of Mr. Will Crooks re- minded me of the time when ".the ,missis " first hit the public .eye, so to put it. The worthy pair lived in a poor neighbourhood in Poplar, and Mrs. Crooks freely devoted her time to helping the distressed and suffering families in the district. She seldom spoke in public. "I prefer," said she, "to talk to the women in their own homes." And, having easily won their confidence, she endeared her- self to them permanently. ?lo Returns.

That bit from last week's "Punch," repro- 'timed. in Saturday's issue of this paper, re- minded me of a funny .sort of fellow whom I met with on a tramcar a while ago. When the man with the bell-punch appeared to col- lect the fares, this person simply said "Return." He seemed much surprised on being told there were no returns—and hardly leas so on finding that it was necessary to .state one's destination before even a single ticket could be obtained. Rather like the one who applied at the railway booking office for "a ticket," and on being asked "What station?" inquired as if in a shop wisiiing to buy a present, "What stations have you?"

Cynicism. Last week's par. about stinting the living and strewing flowers on graves brought to my mind some of the things a brother scribe who was opposed to the use of flowers at funerals used to say. He was wont to avow the belief that "wreaths were ,invented by florists who wanted to make their fortunes with fierce ~eelerity " ; but his criticism did not end with the tradesmen—of some of their customers he would declare that "Many a man sighing for ,publicity has found his opportunity in a wreath." Of course, he was very ill-natured - and quite wrong.

Always Merry and Bright. "Uncle Ned's " timely insistence on the vultivation of the spirit here indicated may just now be emphasised in the case of some older readers. I know it has been said; that happiness is no easy matter—that it is very hard to find it within ourselves and impossible to find it elsewhere. Thus the French pro- verb hath it that he only is happy who thinks he is. Anyliow, Holmes held strongly that there is a place for laughter. "The ludi- ,vrons," wrote he, "has its place in the uni- verse; it is not a human invention, but one of the divine ideas. . . . How curious it is

that we always consider solemnity and the absence of all gay surprises and encounter of wits as essential to the idea of the future life of those whom we thus deprive of half their faculties, and then called blessed!" He went on to refer to certain, " who, even in this life, .seem to be preparing themselves for that smileless eternity to which they look forward by banishing all gaiety from their hearts and all joyousness from their countenances." Of one such whom he often met he adds, "I don't doubt he would cut his kitten's tail off. 'if he caught her playing with it. Please tell me, Who taught her to play with it?"

"Laugh and Grow Fat." This is an old saying, but those who have the misfortune to belong to the class satirised by "The Autocrat" will especially deprecate it in this war time. I invite such to take ox- ample from the cheery, optimism of our irre- pressible soldiers. And, if that be not enough for the more selfish of these self-centred souls, let them consider what a doctor of whom I knew had' to say on the subject some years .ago. Thl, convulsive movements which we call laughter (he asserted) exert a very real effect upon the bodily framework. They cause the arteries to dilate, so that they carry more blood to the tissues of the body, and the heart to beat more rapidly, so that the flow of the blood through the vessels is hastened. In other words, laughter promotes the very best conditions for an increase of the vital pro- cesses; the tissues take up more nutritive material and the waste products are more promptly removed. A good laugh sends an increased flow of blood to the brain; this im- diately causes that instrument of thought to work better, with the result that gloomy fore- bodings are sent packing.. However one looks at it, "Uncle Ned" is undeniably right in tak- ing to task little nephews and nieces who be- tray even a momentary disposition to sad- ness—and at the same time setting them so excellent an example. More Stale Food.

When writing on the subject a week ago I forgot for the moment an occasion when bread eaten was made from wheat found in one of the Egyptian Pyramids, and "grown before the, children of Israel passed through the Red Sea," the butter used with it having been made when Queen Elizabeth was on the throne. The wine drunk was at least 400 years old, and the apples put on for dessert were from the ruins of Pompeii. I remember a party of scientists in Ireland sampling eggs 40 years old, which had been brought from .ehina, where " postponed " eggs are prized as a luxury. But these were left far behind by their Russian brethren. who were once reported to have enjoyed juicy steaks from the body of a mammoth excavated from the frozen ground in Siberia and thus rterfectly preserved, although calculated to have died at least 100,000 years ago Table Manners.

A protest of Dr. Kellogg's against excessive flesh-eating somehow brought to my mind two or three references in contrast. Miss Marie Corelli, who goes in for satire at the expense of Society, writes of their dinners as if the upper ten aped the luxury and the manners of Heliogabalus as portrayed on canvas by Alma-Tadema. No doubt there was a period in our rough island story when the roasts were carried round the table, and each guest cut off what he wanted. They were horribly greedy in those days, and manners were more free than refined; there was no thought of daintiness. But to pretend that there is now anything to correspond with the habits of those times is libellous. The truth lies mid- way between extremes—say, as represented in an essay in which Thackeray devotes pages to the "beauties and excellencies •"• of dinners in Paris. He tells of one which included pheas- ants among other dainties, and cost is. 3d. per head! There was another the description of which I have never forgotten,- although several years have passed since I read it. They had beefsteak and partridge, and when the steak was finished, Thackeray and another Briton who was with him "put bits of bread in the silver. dish and Wistfully sopped up the gravy." But that and greediness are wide -as the poles asunder. An African Menu.

I read that the Rev. P. meson, newly- appointed to the Bold-street Wesleyan cir- cuit, is deeply interested in foreign missions. This, together with the foregoing allusions, prompts a repetition of an African mission- ary's experience of some years ago. This gentleman stated that in making friends with the" nobility" of his district he was some- times invited out, and had the privilege of taking dinner with the king, or one of his chiefs. Then he often wished he could give his sense of taste a holiday, and be able to manufacture eau-de-Cologne on the spot, as he faced the ordeal of pretending to like such delicacies as snail soup, boiled alligator, stewed monkeys, etc.. cooked in palm-oil, a la mode. He did not linger lovingly over the itliah, toying with morsels, and wistfully sop- ping up the gravy.
No man knows anything about heaven who co content that others shall wait for happineee till they get there,

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, 1915.
VENUS IN HIDING.
A New Chapter In The Story Of A Famous Statue.

div.head: ISTORY, TRADITION AND SUPERSTITION.
div.p: ISTORY, TRADITION AND SUPERSTITION.
By ARTHUR

France possesses the most beautiful piece of statuary in the world. So at least every Frenchman will tell you, and after looking upon the famous " Venus de Milo" few will be bold enough to differ. The feeling of the enlightened Frenchman towards the "Venus" is far beyond what may be called affection; he has stood before it in the Louvre in rever- ence and almost in worship. She is a Pagan goddess, it is true, and began her career as such, but she so pleases the eye that neither mind nor heart dare offer a single prejudice. Alas, that we should have to say that Venus is once more in hiding. Not that she herself will mind, for through 18 centuries she lay buried in a cave and must have got used to it. A little more or less can hardly matter. But to her :many admirers it is a thing of deep concern, and those who remem- ber her past remind 'as that she has never been moved without 'being broken. She was hidden away amid strife and lay amid dust and rubbish. As soon as she saw light again her arms were broken off amid the conflicts of men. Now again she is smothered away amid strife and bloodshed, and superstition says there is sure to be another misfortune. Thirteen months ago, when the Germans

div.head: VENUS DE MILO.
div.p: VENUS DE MILO.

were thundering down upnn Paris, Venus of Milo left her home at the Louvre. Large motor vans appeared in the court of the great museum-palace of Paris, and 720 marbles and paintings of all lands and schools and periods —the incomparable treasures of the French nation—were taken away. Venus, who alone weighs 6,600 pounds, had a huge van to herself. Wrapped, packed and smothered in cement, she went to some new adventure. Like many other precious things of the moment, she is " somewhere in France," but whether in city or den or cave of the earth we may not inquire. It is an appropriate moment to think about her. The Venus of Milo or Melos is a Pagan idol, and even in that great day of sculpture must have been one of the very loveliest. Two thousand years ago she probably reigned in a white temple on a hill amid the scenery of a Grecian island, and she reigned as Venus, the Goddess of Love.

Christianity, winning the heathen world, put down the images. Zealots overturned priceless marbles, seeing them only as sym- bols of evil, and failing to see their match- less beauty. But there are those to whom she was dear, and she•was carried away—by stealth perhaps—to a secret vault on a hill- side. She was sealed ,up until a day of resur- rection came, and the stone that hid the entrance was covered with dirt or sod. Beside her in the dark stood two small demons for protection. This was on the island of Melee, an they left her to await another day. That day of resurrection was long deferred, but 'when it did coine. was not lacking in stir 'and drama. div.head: FOOD ECONOMICS.
div.p: FOOD ECONOMICS.
How The Germans Are Utilising Their Waste Land.
VEGETABLES FROM LAKE- BED.
Mr. G. P. Man, managing director of Gartons, Ltd., Warrington, writes us as follows:

So much has recently been written on the subject of food economics that a little insight revealed in an article which appears in the current issue of the "Gardeners' Chronicle" might, I think, we worth putting before those of your readers who take an interest in this phase of our present-day war. problems. _ _ . . . .

Under the title of "Agricultural activity in Berlin," the article referred to reads:— " The citizens of Berlin, represented by the City War Association. for Agriculture, have been making elaborate and careful arrange- ments since the beginning of the year for the cultivation of all available land within the con- fines of Berlin. In January last the Association held its first meeting, and a few weeks later, by diligent co-operation with the municipality and other land-holding corporations, about 700 acres had been. secured. About 200 acres were divided Up into allotments', to be cultivated by poor families under the control of the Associa- tion; the rest; about 500 acres, distributed over various suburbs, was retained to be cultivated under the immediate, direction of the ,Associa- tion itself. : The land Was carefully examined and apportioned by agricultural experts. The major portion was devoted to the cultivation of Potatoes; but a plot of 140 acres, the bed of a lake known as the Tetlow Lake, which had been drained some time previously, was 'rich enough to be suitable for the cultivation of choicer vege- tables. The lake-bottom .was covered with brushwood, nettles and rushes, but this was quickly cleared away by a band of 500 prisoners of war—British and Russian—who. were sup- plied by permission of the military authorities, and worked under the direction of a, guard of Lantlwehr. As soon as the ground was cleared, arrange- ments were made for the training of 250 women and girls—all intelligent and well educated, be- longing to the best Berlin Society—to cultivate the vegetables to be produced. They were

div.head: MOUNFIELD.
div.p: MOUNFIELD.

worked a field on the flank of a hill. The field was in two terraces like steps. On the edge of the upper terrace Yorgos noticed certain big blocks of antique cut stone, and decided to use them. Raising one of them he found a fissure under his feet, into which the dirt rolled. Clearly they were standing above a vault. With the feverish haste of excited men they broke in and saw in the shadows beneath them the figure of a woman in marble. They pushed over a section of the wall into the lower field and jumped in. A strange awe possessed them as they stood before the white goddess, made of cold marble, it is true, yet warm with beauty and natural as-life. Yorgos guessed her value. He knew that old Greek statues had, in foreign eyes, great price, and this statue was entire and perfect. Yes, entire. This is the strange part. Fifty years later Yorgo's son and nephew, who were still alive, protested that she had been found complete. They deelared em- phatically and with details that the Venus, when they found her, was standing upright on her pedestal, the left arm extended and its hand holding an apple. _ _

But her —first contact with the modern world left her a wreck. Yorgos and the two boys • put ihettreasure in safe hiding. They found her to be in two superposed blocks, joined %Visibly at the waist.. /The upper half they hid in a 'cabin and the lower half. was hidden in the vanit- ' A day or twe later the French naval stores ship, La Chevrette, anchored in Melos har- bour. On board was a young ensign, curious of antiquities, who was later to be known to fame as M. Dumont d'Urville. There was an aiiiphitheatre and some tombs on the, island, and he had come to look at them. Moving among the natives he got the news of Yorgos' find. He took aside his friend, Lieutenant Malterer, and suggested that they should go and see

Yorgos was eager to sell and showed them faist of all the legs in the vault. Then they went to the cabin. As then entered a sun- beam from a little window gilded the face and breast of the image. "Rising like a lily from the soil." said D'Urville Venus seemed rising from the cabin floor. in her hand she held an apple. D'Urville agreed to buy. The price was fixed, and the vessel sailed at once to Con- stantinople. The French Ambassador was informed, and in a few days his secretary was sent to make the payment and take posses- sion.

Unhappily before Secretary Marcellus ar- rived some complications had set in. The primates of the islapd had taken it upon themselves to make a gift of the 'Venus to a Greek prince in Constantinople. So Yorgos had sold to them also, and half the purchase had been paid. The French war schooner, L'Estafetto, sent by the French Ambassador, arrived in Melos harbour, May 23rd, 1820. Another brig, flying the Turkish flag, was anchored there, and the commander, to his consterna- tion, saw a crowd of Greek and Turkish soldiers laboriously carrying the upper half of the statue towards the beach. The com- mander grasped the situation. The prize was being carried away before his eyes. There was time to arm a squad of marines and to row to the shore in a long boat. The Turkish crew had also taken in the. situation, and another long boat full of armed men reached the beach at the same moment. Cutlasses and clubs opened the fight. The Turks dropped the Venus to defend themselves. A Turkish ear was slashed off, and thinking this was carnage enough, the Turks backed off and left the Frenchmen standing over the marble. They bribed the Turks, who ceded them the lower half, and the two parts were rowed to the ship.

But Venus bore sad wounds. Indeed she was most wounded of all who shared in the fight. Fragments of marble were gathered from the beach, but whether they belonged to arms or legs was beyond the wit of man. The beautiful left arm, which they said had held the apple, was hopelessly crushed. Venus was placed in the Louvre, and ever since has been its crowning ornament. FrOm then until now artists have tried to replace those arms without success. She has been posed with a shield resting upon her knee, with a mirror, with an apple; but ,no one has made a convincing picture: The conundrum of the placing of the arms is unsolved, and she stands chidingly with ugly stumps to reprove men for the folly of their warring and intrigue. Each time she has been moved it has been because of the clash of arms, and they say that each time she has received a fresh and ugly wound. In 1870, when the Germans swooped down upon Paris, she was hurried into the cellars of the Louvre.
.This time she has gone on a journey, and the place of her sepulchre only the official man knoweth. But she has been wrapped by loving hands, and will come back unscathed! We shall see.

Each dozen students is under the direction of a fully qualified woman gardener. Punctually at seven in the morning they begin their work, continuing until eleven, and at three in the afternoon they recommence, to cease work for the day at seven p.m. All of them are giving their services free and work with great energy. div.head: LESSON FOR US.
div.p: A LESSON FOR US.

Owing to the vigilance of our Navy, which enables us to continue the command of the seas and thus ensure our full supplies of all kinds of food, we are happily not in such " straits " as the apostles of " kultur " for our means of sustenance. This information, how- ever, shows the energy and resourcefulness of our enemy in a direction which although for reasons already- stated needs no compulsion on our part, nevertheless indicates how much more might be made of land which, although suit- able for the production of cereal or vegetable foods, may at the present time not be made full use of. More attention on our part to this question, which is not an unimportant one, would be in the direction of bringing us into line with those nations which are distinctly more 'self-supporting than we are. • It would further assist the thrift campaign, which we are told is more than desirable if we are to
meet the enormous expenditure that is at pre-- sent necessary for the successful conduct of the -war.

div.head: FOLLOW THE KING!
div.p: FOLLOW THE KING!
Closing Meetings In Pledge. Signing Campaign.
"EFFICIENCY."

The Warrington Citizens' Temperance League on Wednesday evening and last night held the two closing meetings in their war pledge-signing campaign. Wednesday night's meeting was held at the junction of Knutsford-road and Thel- wall-lane, where a crowd assembled.

div.head: WATCHWORD.
div.p: THE WATCHWORD.

Mr. A. H. Cox, who presided, said they were out to appeal to the spirit of patriotism which they knew the people possessed. We were pass- ing through the most serious crisis in the history of the Motherland; four Allies fighting against a relentless and powerful foe. In four points— men, munitions, money, morale—were they fighting shoulder to shoulder, determined to secure victory at whatever cost in the shortest time possible. To this end " Efficiency " was the watchword; and one thing which would ensure this efficiency was total abstinence, and he was sorry to say that in that matter we were lagging behind. Our great Allies had already realised the results of drink prohibition; they took the initiative because they realised the supreMe crisis of the moment and determined to add one factor to the eralisation of ultimate victory. And they had believed,' and still be- lieved, that our own Government should have taken drastic action in the early stages of the war and follow the example of our brave Allies and np less the example of our own noble Sovereign, and do away with the sale of intoxi- cants—if only for the duration of the war. He said efficiency was the watchword; and that would not only make for efficiency in the Army and Navy, but filso in all branches of the civil. population. The moral effects of drink upon society and our national life were beyond description, and never could the ambitions of this country be realised whilst intoxicants were allowed to play havoc in our industrial life. We must make not our ideal low gratification and self-indulgence in these times, but be loyal I and devoted; thus, we could depend upon it, would be secured for us the ultimate victory which our hearts called for and aimed for. Miss Ada Hamer then sang very sweetly " Bring Home Your Money To-nig—."

div.head: ENEMY TO CITIZENSHIP.
div.p: ENEMY TO CITIZENSHIP.

Mr. Benjamin T. Parkes, the well-known local temperance reformer, said they were out that night because we had an enemy in our midst. Wherever we went to-day we saw some of our fellow-citizens clad in the King's uniform; one could not enter a train or even scarcely a Warrington tram without seeing them—millions of young men, and some a little older, who had gone forth at the call to fight the enemy of almost the whole world. Now we were not all able to go and fight the enemy without, but we could all fight the enemy with- in ; and he would give several reasons, why they believed alcoholic liquor to be an enemy to citizenship.

div.head: Impairs Nation's Health.
div.p: Impairs Nation's Health.

Our country at present wanted the best out of every man and woman, whether soldier or citizen: and the man who dabbled with alcoholic drink could not give of his very best, because it had been established that such liquor inter- fered with our health. We had it on the highest medical authority, and the military authorities told us that to be efficient a man must abstain. We had it from Lord Kitchener, who appealed to every citizen not to give a soldier drink; in the House of Commons Mr. Asquith said that of the soldiers being trained at least five per cent. were being interfered with because people would persist in taking alcoholic drink. In our country the Friendly Societies had to issue returns to the Registrar-General; and he told us that if we would take the ages of 25 to 65—the forty best years of our lives— the total abstinence section (Rechabites) , had 29 weeks- less sickness than the general mem- bers of the other societies who were not avowed total abstainers: when we remembered that in those other sections a great many did not drink, we could see the percentaW of sickness amongst those who did! They would be healthier with- out alcohol, and therefore bound to be more efficient for giving the country just what she asked for.
Liberty And Citizenship.

Then we should be happier without alcohol; and to be happy we must have our freedom somewhere, There was no commodity which interfered with man's freedom more than liquor. Sometimes we had seen it in the papers —especially in letters to our editor—that total abstinence would interfere with the liberty of the subject; but there was nothing interfered with liberty as much as drink. Drink placed men and women in our Workhouses and Unions, where they were not living a free life: it would surprise some to see the marks and traits upon some of the faces there. Their citizenship was for the time being taken away from them; and the majority were there through liquor. Another branch where men were taken through alco- holic liquor was the asylums; we were told by the superintendents. We were also told that insanity, "that most dreadful of diseases, was most often the result of. brain-poisoning, the chief of which was alcohol." And then our prison houses! Here we found again that liquor was the greatest factor in depriving men and women of their citizenship and confining them. We had only to ask our Chief Constable for one of his reports. Take that for 1913 for instance, and we found that out of 1,400 cases dealt with. altogether 500 of them were directly on account of alcoholic drink; and if we went through the report we should see that many of the other cases were indirectly. Then think of its social effect upon our women and children! Was it not a scandalous shame that there was in this country to-day the necessity of such a society Mr the prevention of cruelty to children? Yet children had suffered cruelly and been neg- lected. and the superintendent of that Society' said that the majority of cases—once even 90 per cent.—were directly caused through drink. Where The Government Fails.

Should the war last a long time (which they hoped it would not!) and we kefir our pledges, he believed we should be so glad with the results that we should never again touch drink. We would save three million pounds a week for ourselves, and thus for the country; and just now the call was one to thrift. If the Parlia- mentary Committee which had been appointed to tell the people how to save would be honest they would ask people in all fairness to them- selves to give up the drink. They had done something by giving Chief Constables power to close public-houses early should they consider it necessary, but that was not sufficient; then the military authorities stepped in too; but that was. not sufficient. The time had come when the Government ought to take stronger measures against our common foe Alcohol; we ought not as a nation to allow any trade to stand in front of our life, and because of its powerful influence say it should not be touched or handled.

When we could say that the Union Jack—the flag of honour, the,,flag of liberty, the flag of thith—still floated, then after the people had got over their rejoicing let them have the choice of saying whether this enemy should be allowed to remain in our midst again. Until the Government did what it ought to, they appealed to every man and woman to do what they could themselves—sign the pledge! The speech was followed by some questions and discussion.

div.head: MR. JOSEPH ALLISON.
div.p: MR. JOSEPH ALLISON.
Well-known Bowler-Licensee Passes Away.

At the age 'of 63, Mr. Joseph Allison passed away at his residence, 386, Manchester-road, Warrington, on Tuesday morning at 2 o'clock. We • state the newewith regret. For, ten weeks Mr. Allison had been ill, and passed away despite the attentions of Dr. Joseph—leaving widow, one brother and two sisters to mourn him.

A lifelong resident of Warrington, the de- ceased gentleman was the son of the late Mr. James Allison, of Church-street; and wor- shipped at the Parish Church. He first entered employment at Messrs. Rylands Bros., Ltd., leaving in 1870, when he joined (under the man- agement of the late Mr. Frederick Monks) the Whitecross Works. Mr. Allison presently be- came licensee of the Gladstone Arms, Church- street, transferring nine years later to the Cemetery Hotel. Here he remained for 21 years, retiring only a year or two ago.

div.head: FORTY YEARS' RECORD.
div.p: FORTY YEARS' RECORD.

In the bowling art, Mr. Allison's interest and proficiency, became noticeable with,in a com- paratively few 'years of his coming' here at 'an early age from Droylesden. As a young man he was wont to take part in—and win—many handicaps; in fact, he had always proved a successful bowler.' It was so. far, back as 1869 that lie commenced his association with the Cemetery Hotel Green—little thinking, perhaps, that in future years-he was to have control of it, and in these handicap successes he started to participate within five years' time., In the first he ran up to the final in the closing main, when be was defeated by Mr. Peter Wells, head of the well-known family of bowlers. In 1875 he gained a aeries of successes at mains in the town and district, establishing thereby his reputation as a bowler, and in 1896 he crowned everything by becoming the amateur cham- pion of Lancashire and Cheshire. In this his opponent was Mr. J. W. G. Coombes, after- wards president of the British Crown Green Association. For this championship he had also been the runner-up. The Cemetery Bowl- ing Club team that on two occasions carried off the Lancashire County Cup he represented, and for a series of years was a member of the county team. Also he was a member of the Cemetery Club's team when it won the War- rington and District Bowling Cup. When two years ago he retired, Mr. Allison had a bowling record of no less than forty years, and the club took the opportunity of presenting him with a handsome inscribed clock. At the same time the Licensed Victuallers—with whose movement he was associated, having served on the Executive Committee for 21 years. and being also a trustee—gave him a fine silver table centrepiece. In his youth Mr. Allison was a member and worker of St. Ann's Church, and belonged to the St. Ann's Rifle Band when that movement was running. Also possessed of a fine tenor voice, he earned much popularity at local social functions.
It is interesting to note that Mrs. Allison— who also was greatly interested in bowls—was (assisted by her husband) the pioneer of the ladies' mains inaugurated at the Cemetery Hotel in 1904.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
THE YEAR'S CROPS.
A Remarkable Recovery And
Good Results.

"The Times" special report on the state of this year's crops is, on the whole, a satisfactory one. The, system adopted is to allow 100 to represent perfect healthfulness in a crop and the reporters give an idea of how much the crop in a certain district approximates to that state by the 'employment of relatively corre- sponding figures. The position of perfection has on this occasion been attained for wheat in Lancashire and Monmouth; and for potatoes in Lancashire and Northumberland. These are exceptions, but individual reporters in very many cases record 105, 110, or even higher figures, which are, however, too often pulled down by adverse reports from the same county. The general result of the inquiry seems to be that wheat and barley improved slightly dur- ing August, in spite of rough and inclement weather, while oats gained several points. On the other hand, potatoes lost 2.6 points, and beans sank to even a lower level than they had reached at the close of July. The most encouraging features of the present report are found in the extraordinary improvement in pastures, and the recovery of swedes and tur- nip? from practically _zero on July 1 to quite a fair' average prospect on September 1. All these changes are due- to the weather. Autumn-sown crops, whether of wheat, oats, or beans, are comparatively independent of the vicissitudes of spring and early summer, and the reporters frequently give two figures. In one they may estimate winter oats 100 and spring oats at 50 or 60; or winter beans at 100 while the spring-sown crop is put at 25, 50, or event reported trze be a complete failure. Root crops, being mostly sown in May, June, and July, escape the effects of a dry and late spring, and are ready to take advantage of showery weather, such as we experienced in July and August. Grass is always ready to grow at any season of the year, provided the conditions are favourable. illence we have good crops of- winter corn, of roots, potatoes, and grass; and poor crops of spring-sown oats, barley and beans.

On the Ist September our principal crops stood as follows, the average in each case for the last ten years being stated in parenthesis : Wheat, 94 (against a ten year average of 93.9); barley, 86.6 (90.8); oats, 87.2 (87.2); beans, 80.5 (88.1); potatoes, 91.4 (89.9); turnips and swedes, 86.4 (86.8). It will be seen that wheat end oats are average crops; that barley and beans are decidedly under average; and that grass, roots, and 'potatoes are satisfactory, although potatoes are threatened.

div.head: Lancashire's Wheat Record.
div.p: Lancashire's Wheat Record.

The local fluctuations are very considerable. The highest records for wheat are those of Kent, Sussex, Monmouth, Devon and Lancashire, while the lowest are from Cambridge, Lincoln, Norfolk and Suffolk, all four of which work out below 90 per cent. of a full and satisfactory crop: Monmouth heads the list for wheat with uniform reports-of 100 from six leading agricul- turists of the county. _ _

Figures indicate' an average 'crop of wheat Over the entire country, and give the impres- sion of a splendid crop injured by wind, rain and hail. Lancashire figures :—Wheat, 102; barley, 100; oats, 85; beans —; potatoes, 100; roots (except mangels), 87. Cheshire figures Wheat, 95; barley, 88; oats, 77; beans —; potatoes, 83; roots (excebt mangels) 68.

div.head: Silver Year.
div.p: A Silver Year.

In many other countries on September 1 the harvest was far advanced. Wheat is the crop of the year—" a silver year," as an Usk corre- spondent calls it. Barley is very disappointing,, and works out four points below the average of the previous 10 years. The most discouraging feature is, that the lowest averages hail from the biggest barley- growing counties. Oats have at last achieved the position of being an average crop, after having been stigmatized in the July report as "one of the worst on record." Potatoes have advanced from 87 in July to 91.4. on September Ist, which is a, remarkable improvement. They are, however, threatened by disease, which was prevalent (September Ist), as far north as Cheshire and Stafford. Mange' is a fine crop, working out to the satisfactory figure of 90.3 for England, 90 for Wales, and 95.7 for Scotland. There is, there- fore, every prospect of a plentiful supply of roots for the cbming winter.

Concurrently with roots, grass and grazing prospects have gone up like. a rocket from 66 on July Ist to 90 for England, 100 for Wales, and from 76 to 92.5 for Scotland. Second crops of clover-hay are also reported upon as excep- tionally good. All kinds of fodder are, there- fore, likely to be abundant.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
AUTUMN FLOWERS.

There is very often a lack of colour in the garden at this time of the year owing to too much dependence on purely summer flowering plants that are liable to collapse from the early autumn storms. There Ls no necessity for such lack of bloom as there is a great wealth of autumn flowering plants that will stanerough gales. It only needs a little careful selection to make the garden as bright in the autumn days as in the summer, with this advantage, that the summer flowering plants need annual propaga- tion, sowing or transplanting, while those that may be relied on for the autumn display need very little attention after they are planted. In fact, the longer, in many cases, they are allowed to stand the more effective they are, the only thing they require being a good top-dressing of manure in the winter. Given this attention they will grow freely, and in their season give a rich display of bloom. On visiting a friend's garden in the suburbs the other day (September Ist) I found the following in bloom :—The Japanese anemone, dahlias (single and double), gladioli, sunflowers, early flowering chrysanthe- mums, sedum spectabile, torch lilies, phloxes, everlasting peas, hollyhocks, aster Thomsoni, bee balm, erigeron speciosus, to mention only a few.

div.head: LIVE EDGINGS.
div.p: LIVE EDGINGS.

The mossy saxifrages, thrift, London pride, and stonecrops make excellent edgings, as they are not cold and hard like the tiles one so often sees, used. A very handsome edging may be made of pieces of stone—andstone for pre- ference—over- which sedums, saxifrages, the dwarf campanulas, aubrietias, tufted pansies; and many other dwarf growing plants may be allowed to grow and hide the stones. In country gardens the gentianella may be used as an edging, its mat-like growth fitting it well for this purpose. The common thrift makes a fine edging, pleasing to look at all seasons, being rich green during the winter and when in bloom a mass of rich pink colour. London pride is on,i of the most useful edging plants for a garden, even when not in bloom, while 'when tarrying its billowy masses of flowers, pinky-white, it is always admired, though some may call it com- mon- People have an idea that the London pride will be content in the poorest soil. This is true in a sense, but give the plants a good larder and note the great difference in the num- ber and length of the flowering spikes.

div.head: IVY UNDER TREES.
div.p: IVY UNDER TREES.

• It is often very difficult to find a suitable plant to cover the soil under trees where grass will not grow. Ivy, if carefully planted and care taken to train it over the ground for the first year or two will answer in most cases. Planters should always bear in mind that close Up to the boles of large trees there can be no moisture, hence it is of no avail to plant anything close up to these. The only way to get ivy to grow under trees is to make holes for the roots out- side the line of drip. Make the .pits large enough to hold two or three bushels of good loamy soil, to which has been added some rich, well rotted manure. After planting and well treading the soil give a good soaking of water. The ivy plants, which can always be had in pots, may be set out at a distance of from 3ft. to sft. apart. The shoots of the ivy should be directed inwards, carefully and frequently pegged down until the bole of the tree is reached. No matter how barren the ground under the trees, the ivy will grow away freely if the roots are provided for in thd way just described. When thoroughly well established the tips of the growths may be cut off, causing the shoots to break back and the more thickly cover the ground.—Wick, in " Farm and Home."

div.head: CRUSHED BY BUFF:4: S.
div.p: CRUSHED BY BUFF:4: S.
Fatal Shunting Accident At The Pearson & Knowles' Works.

Coroner Brighouse conducted an inquest at the Borough Police Station on Wednesday on the body of Wm. Johnston Keddie, who was fatally crushed between-railway waggons whilst assisting in shunting operations for Messrs. Pearson and Knowles at their Hoop Mill siding on Monday. Evidence of identification having been given by the widow, the Coroner submitted to the jury plans and photographs illustrating the manner of the occurrence of the tragedy. How It Happened.

The first evidence as to the accident was given by Edwin Shoebridge, engine-driver in the em- ploy of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, and living at 240, Knutsford-road4 He stated that he had been twenty years with the firm and twenty years in the Army. At 12.10 on Monday, he said, he was engaged in shunting operations at Hoop Mill siding. There were two waggons in the siding, and the object was to get one wag- gon away. The full waggon was fouling the points, and a prop had to be used to get it to go in the right direction. Whilst the prop was being thus used to ease the waggon over the points, it slipped and the deceased was pitched forward between the buffers and badly crushed. Witness went about three or four yards after the prop slipped. The deceased sat down and the doctor was sent for and ordered his removal to the Infirmary.

In reply to the Coroner, witness said there was no other way of doing the job except by the use of a. prop. Answering the question of Mr. C. H. Una- worth (acting for Mr. T. S. Steel, who repre- sented the widow); witness said deceased had been twelve months on the job. He was doing something quite usual in using the prop. The Coroner: He was standing in the right position, and it was only the prop that put hint into danger? Witness: Yes.

div.head: Only Way.
div.p: The Only Way.

Mr. H. Greenall (representing the firm): You were using that prop because of the impossi- bility of doing the work in any other way, owing to the fact that a new building was being erected in a certain position? Witness: Yes.
It was not a usual course of procedure, but has only been in use since the building has been in course of erection?—No. It was necessary on account of the building. -

John Young, foreman shunter, corroborated the evidence of the last witness. Deceased, he added, was carrying out his duty quite properly. and using the prop was the only way the work could be done. The temporary process had bees necessary since Wednesday of the prevloo4 week. The Factory Inspector (Mr. H. E. Brothers)' Does it rest with you whether you use the proP or take some other means of moving the wag" gons? • Witness: Yes, it does, really.
And you understand that if there is nnf other way of moving the waggons, you don't use the prop?—Yes. The only reason you used the nrop in this case was that there was no other alternative? --- Yes.
Mr. Unsworth: Then he was acting under your superintendence in ,using the prop? Witness: Yes. Couldn't the waggons have been moved bi two or three men pushing them?—No!

div.head: Never Slipped Befdre.
div.p: Never Slipped Befdre.
You have done this before, without any AP. parent danger to the man. using the prop?—Yes, six or seven times.

And the prop has never slipped before?—N° The Inspector said that the use of the proP was recognised to be dangerous, and was Pro. hibited by the law, if there was any other means available. In that particular case, lie was satisfied that resorting to the prop was the only way of doing the work. The jury having returned a verdict of " Acci- dental death," Mr. Greenall, on behalf of the firm, expressed sympathy with the widow and children. Deceased had been seven years Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' employ. - The Coroner acknowledged the help the firm had given the Court by supplying the plans and photographs; which, he said, lied assisted the jury, to arrive at a correct conclusion.

div.p: Death Alters The Outlook.

The Rev. H. Ogden selected as the basis of his discourse the words :" And the sea gave up the dead which were in it. And there was no more sea" (Revelations xx. 13; and xxi. 1). It was, he said, a curious suggestion that there should be no more sea, until we came to analyse it. Even in these times, when we were in the midst of warfare, men tired and worn by physical labours had sought and obtained re- cuperation from the sea- From the grim toil and the rattle of the factory they had sought the seclusion and peace of the. seashore. Not only was the body refreshed, but the soul had been awakened. No more glorious vision had been revealed to man than a sunset at sea. To the average man the sea meant health and vision. But circumstances considerably altered the outlook. Some of those who were gathered there that night could never look again upon the sea with the same feeling as ere it shrouded their hallowed ones. They thought of those dear forms as lying with the seaweeds for a shroud, and though it meant health and strength to others, it would remind them of a great tragedy and sorrow in their own lives.

div.head: No More Sea.
div.p: No More Sea.

John said i "There shall be no more sea." To him it had been a prison. When he longed to be at work amongst the churches, the waves washed around his lonely prison at Patmos, and when the vision of a new heaven was re- vealed to him there was to be no more sea. In that beautiful Gloryland there was to be no hindrance, no disappointment, no sad remind- ers. And it was glorious to think that in that beautiful city he would not be hindered by autocracies and monarchies. There would be no haunting memories; there would be. no more sea. With all his mastery' .of- air- and ocean, the great elements still remained unconquered by man, and frightful disasters occasionally reminded us of the enormous power of air and ocean.
The Body Not The Individual.

The men who were on the Royal Edward when she went down had trusted in the security of her greatness and in hardly more than a, moment of time they passed from sleep to the Gloryland. If the sea was to keep its dead, then some of our noblest sacrifices would be in vain. They cherished the sure hope for those who slept in the Lord. True it was that the earthly case was dear to us; but it was not the earthly case that made the life of those two brothers—John Barnett and Stanley Monks. The mere case was not the individual. The individual was the soul, and the moment when the body lost its vitality was the moment when the soul was greater than the mighty ocean. The Compulsion of Duty.

One felt anxious to pay a tribute, if only a small one, to the heroism of those two brethren. They were both volunteers. No compulsion save the compulsion to duty for the highest called them to the Colours..., One of them, ere taking up his duty in the war, had selected an occupation that demanded heroism—the foot- plate of an express engine was no place for a man who was unsteady and unstable in his ways—and had he been spared the very hero- ism he had shown in warfare would have mani- fested itself in civil life for the nation's good. The parents of those lads were suffering, but let them remember for what they had died. They had shown themselves ready to bleed and die that righteousness might reign in the earth; and nothing was more sure than the immor- tality of the brave.

div.head: APPRENT!CES' PAY.
div.p: APPRENT!CES' PAY.
Trades Council Favours Uniform Basis.

At the monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday night, there was some discussion on a circular letter received from the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation of Trades and Labour Councils with regard to the rate of wages paid to apprentices.

The Federation's letter ;et forth that that body had discussed the matter and it was agreed by the delegates that ;even the highest paid apprentice was seriously under-rated. The rates had been in operation and unrevised, for a number. of years, and -despite 'advances that had been secured in almost every trade and calling, the apprentice remained where he was many years ago. The Federation, therefore, thought the time overdue when the Unions should seriously undertake the establishment of ap- prentice rates upon a uniform basis and some- what commensurate with the cost of mainten- ance. It was no longer advisable that employers should have the advantage of cheap apprentice labour, but that immediately a youth entered a trade, rates vshould be fixed by his Society, of which he should immediately become a mem- ber, so as to graduate his scale of payment, culminating with the maximum amount at the expiration of his apprentice period. At pre- sent there was no uniformity in payment, and in some trades the apprentice was scarcely recognised until his third or fourth year. "If greater care and attention" concluded, the letter, "were bestowed upon these future Trade Unionists they would become better members of their Society and amply compensate for any services given during their early connection with the trade."

div.head: APPRENTICES AND THE WAR.
div.p: APPRENTICES AND THE WAR.

The Burnley Trades and Labour Council wrote asking whether the Warrington Trades and Labour Council had taken any action with regard to the matter of apprentices and war allowances, the Lancashire . and Cheshire Federation having pointed out that from every trade, large numbers of apprentices between the age of 18 and 21 have joined, the Colours. "If," the Federation circular continued, "we assume the war is likely to continue for two or three years, these young men will have given their service to the country, but at the same time will have deprived themselves of the know- ledge and skill necessary for the pursuance of their craft. The Council might. bring notice of this to the affiliated Societies so that steps might be taken to assure the return of these young men to their former occupation. Special rates and conditions covering a probationary perio.l will necessarily' have to be arranged between the Societies and the firms. where they are employed. Unless steps are taken in this direc- tion we fear that numbers of these young fellows will drift into the unskilled labour market and their earning capacity be seriously impaired." The Council decided to take steps along the lines indicated in the Federation's letter.

Money From Old Jewellery. The Bank of France has hit upon an excellent method of raising money for the national defence, and at the same time of helping .the necessitous citizens of all classes. An arrange- ment has been made with the French Mint to purchase old or broken pieces of gold jewellery, payment being given for its full value. There is an enormous amount of old and modern jewellery in France, for savings—more especially in the South—are still turned into bracelets. ear-rings and necklaces. The French peasants, in common with those of Italy, consider these investments safer than a bank. As every class is suffering more or less from the war, many people are only too glad to dispose of useless and broken gold ornaments, and already large quan- tities have been converted into bullion. No charge is made for the transactions, and a certificate is given to each seller to show that he or she has paid in so many grammes of gold for the national defence.

Historic Toys. Perhaps the most comprehensive and unique collection of toys and playthings has been made by Mr. Edward Lovett, of Croydon. In this collection toys and playthings of all ages and all countries have been gathered together, and it is a matter of congratulation that the owner has presented the results of many years labour to the Stepney Borough Council. The gift in- cludes ingenious playthings that amused the babies of China and India long before London was foundeil. Dolls, tea sets and cooking utensils of this period are in many instances artistically designed and well finished. Rough clay models of toys in use ages ago, primitive carts, wagons,' and wigwams of semi-savage races, are all represented. The collection has been brought up-to-date, the latest mechanical toys forming no inconsiderable part of it. Doctor Dee's Black Stone.
Astrology and astronomy were, until modern times twin sciences, and the astrologer was a person of the greatest importance, not only. in

Eastern, but in Western Courts. The predic- tions of astrologers of mediveval times affected the market value of property and securities, much as the Stock Exchange is affected by political events and rumours. Queen Elizabeth placed great confidence in the famous Doctor Dee, and in order that he might have the necessary funds to continue his search for the elixir of life, granted him at various times large sums of money. Doctor Dee possessed a "black stone" credited with remarkable powers. This stone is to be sold at Christies for a charity. Napoleon placed great faith in the crystal, and one he possessed and used frequently is now in the possession of Queen Alexandra. Pleats For Autumn Dresses.

Heavy materials cannot be used for full skirts without danger to health, therefore the moder- ately wide garment is to be worn in cold weather. Where heavy cloths are chosen the weight will be sustained .partly from the shoulder. Several Princess designs have braces under which thin blouses are worn, matching the dress in colour, but of a very light material. This arrangement decreases the weight very considerably. Pleats are quite a feature of autumn dresses. There appears to be no set rule as to where they must be placed, but they are more frequently seen at the sides than at the front or back. Again they may be-intro- duced just below the knee, in this case the skirt is moderate in width, and fares at the sides only enough for comfort in walking. A graceful and youthful skirt for present wear has a front panel, and three circular flounces. This skirt measures not more than three yards, the foundation being in three pieces.

Stripes Still Popular. Striped materials have much to recommenti them. They do not show the dust, they are therefore practical and economical. Also they are pleasing to the eye, give variety to .-%. ere styles, and add, when judiciously In inipulated— to the apparent height of the w,•arer. These advantages doubtless account for the popularity they continue to enjoy. In, stone awl bPige tints, in grey and brown shades, as well as in other colours, contrasted or 'combined, striped clothes will be. worn throughout the- coming winter. A material that is meeting with much favour, among tailors, is a rather heavy makA of whipcord, trimmed with black or coloured
d

velvet. Hems of the latter fabric often take the place of fur, when collars and cuffs are of velvet. Suits in covert coating are as popular as serge, for present wear, and the newest makes are altogether charming. Not only can this serviceable material be obtained in stone colour, rich browns and other shades, but in various heather mixtures. The latter are among the novelties of the autumn season.

Autumn And Summer Lingerie. Corsets and underwear, although invisible, play a very important part in the scheme of dress, and this will always be so, for unless they take the lines of the silhouette, disaster is inevitable. Therefore lingerie should be bough': in moderate quantities only; it can then be replaced every season or two. The flare and fullness of the skirts of to-day are reflected in all under-garments prepared for the autumn and winter. Envelope chemises that every day become more popular, combinations, drawers, and of course petticoats, are all considerably wider at the hem than a year ago, and they are far more comfortable for the extra width. Many materials are now used for lingerie that 'fifty years ago would have been considered impos- sible. Take chiffon, crepe de chene, China silk and cotton crepe, for instance. For serviceable underwear, the fine makes of longeloth are hard to beat, and for summer wear fhis old- fashioned material has been much in evidence. It is soft, has a closer weave than nainsook, and is lighter than cambric. It is also reasonable in price, and very durable, two admirable qualities in these expensive times. A Moth Proof Bag. A wet summer always bring more moths than a dry one, and this year they are more than usually in evidence, whilst some towns have also suffered from plagues of ants and mosquitoes. It is possible to buy moth-proof bags, which can be hermetically closed, and are provided with hooks on which to hang the garmentt. Equally effective is the bag which can be made at home out of newspapers. If trouble is taken to see that there are no holes, and that all the edges are folded over and carefully gummed down, it is as good a device as any for protecting the con- tents from injuries of all kinds. There is some- thing in printers' ink which moths dislike, and the newspaper bag is not only as safe as any, but it helps to keep moths away from ward- robes or drawers, in which it is placed.

An Old Plan of Preserving Apples and Pears. An old plan especially useful with apples and pears may be described. Prepare a solution in the Proportion of one pound 'resin, one ounce tallow, and one ounce beeswax. Put the items in an iron saucepan and set over a fire. .The melting should take place slowly, and the mix- ture should not boil. Each fruit must be taken separately and rubbed over with whiting or preoipitated chalk. In order to dip the fruits into the solution, put a pointed stick into each. After dipping, hold the fruit in the air for a moment so that the thin coating of solution may set; if desired the, wood chip can be cut down to the fruit, though it should not be pulled out, as this would let the air in. After treatmei# put away on shelves or in boxes. When required for use, it is only necessary to crack the coating and peel it away. It will be found that the fruits are beautifully preserved owing to the fact that the air has been kept away.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticul- tural Review."

Cottage Pie. , Take the remains of a leg of mutton, two blades of pounded mace, a dessertspoonful of chopped parsley, a teaspoOnful of minced savoury herb e a little onion, if liked, four Potatoes, a cupful of gravy, pastry to Cover the 'pie. Pour in the gravy, cover with a good short suet crust, and bake for one hour.

Stewed Mutton With Haricot Beans. One lb. of lean mutton-, loz. of butter or good dripping, one large onion, half a pint of haricot beans, one quart of water, pepper and salt. Cut the mutton in pieces, slice the onion. Put the batter into an iron saucepan Over the tire, and when it is quite hot fry the onion and mutton slightly brown, add pepper and 'salt with the beans, which Must have been pre- viously prepared—that is, well washed, the dark ones thrown away, and soaked in plenty of cold water for twelve hours, and then washed again in fresh *cold water. Pour on the water, stir until boiling, skim well, and let simmer for two hours, or until the beans are tender. Serve the beans around a dish with the mutton in the centre.

div.head: Baked Macaroni.
div.p: Baked Macaroni.

Quarter .of a pound of macaroni, boil 20 minutes or till soft in salted water, drain in a colander and pour water through it; then cut 'in inch pieces and put into a baking-dish, season with half a teaspoonful. of salt, half a saltspoonful of cayenne, two tablespoonfuls of grated cheese, if liked. Pour over the whole three gills of white sauce and cover that with two-thirds of a cupful of breadcrumbs moistened in a third of a cupful of butter. melted. Bake

haps twelve, possibly fifteen, minutes to brown the crumbs.

Curried Eggs. Put into a saucepan an ounce of salt butter, a tablespoonful of chopped onion, and cook till they are brown. Then stir in two dessert- spoonfuls of curry powder, mixing it well, add two dessertspoonfuls of flour, stirring quickly all the time. Add a quarter of a pint of milk and water, and when a good sauce is made put in four hard-boiled eggs cut in slices. Serve with boiled rice.

div.head: Our Minds Need Work.
div.p: Our Minds Need Work.

While ive must protect our minds by avoiding any injury to our nervous forces, still we must actively exercise our minds if we are to strengthen them and lead them to the fullest development of which they are capable, com- ments a writer in "Leslie's Weekly." A brain and its corresponding mind will become weak if it is not used, just as surely as a muscle will waste and weaken if it has no exercise. Our minds should have suitable occupation and proper work to do. Many of the people who apply to physicians for a rest cure really need a work cure more. Properly ordered work does not hurt the mind, but helps it.

There is, however, such a thing as over- exertion; it is by no means uncommon among our high-strung, ambitious and ovemonscien- tious people, and leads to nervous exhaustion and all physical and mental evils which this condition carries in its train. Our efforts to strengthen the mind by exercise are defeated if we think only of the work and neglect proper nutrition and suitable intervals of rest and diversion. The strong mind is not made in haste, but results from a long, slow and sensible training. Good sleep at night, restful recreation 'Sundays and holidays, enjoyable exercise in the orcn air are essential to it

div.head: HINTh ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTh ON HEALTH.
Useful Information In Popular Language.
Foods To Build Up The Body.

In a thoroughly practical article on this sub- ject, Dr. T. D. Crothers says in "Good Health": " Men and women, ignorant of the purpose and value of foods, keep filling the stomach with heat products. A surplus of sugar, fats, and starches will not build up the body and brain. Proteids or albumen found in wheat, rice, and oats, and in meats are necessary. Beans, :leas and lentils contain more building up food properties than any kind of meat, pound for pound, but they are rather hard to digest in considerable quantity. Meats are the most ex- pensive foods and the least valuable in propor- tion to tost and are sure to be discarded in the near future to a large extent, both from expense and from the enormous waste that they take into the body, which must be thrown' off, and which requires energies that ought to be used in other directions."

Clothing The Body And Its Effects. Clothing has a very much more direct bearing upon the functions of the colon that might at first be supposed. Corsets and belts tend directly to produce constipation by hampering the movements of the diaphragm, by preventing proper development and activity of the abdo- minal muscles, and by causing displacement of the colon and other viscera into the lower por- tion of the abdomen. Excess of clothing tends th produce the same results by overheating the body and producing excessive perspiration and relaxation of the muscular structures of the abdomen, and perhaps also of the. intestines. The only relief is to be found in discarding all clothing that has a restrictive effect upon any of the parts of the body, and making the clothes so loose that the body has the utmost freedom for all its movements.

Beauty And Health. Health is the foundation of beauty. To be really beautiful, one's beauty must be more than skin deep. Do not be satisfied with the beauty that is deep enough merely to deceive the superficial Onlooker. It was Aristotle who said that beauty of figure is far more to be admired than mere beauty of face. This means that one must have not only a beautiful face, but beautiful hands as well; not only a good complexion for the face, but a good complexion ail over. The writer was very much shocked, in examining a young lady with a beautiful face, to find that ' her back was covered all over will pimples. When told what they signified, she said, lightly, "If it was on my face I should feel awfully bad about it, but as long as it is out of sight I don't mind it." But pimples on the back mean the same thing as pimples on the face— uncleanness inside; the whole body is in a state of uncleanness, .and of low resistance because of this inner uncleanness. The only way to be really beautiful is to live beautifully, to live rightly. If one is going to be beautiful, for , example, one must eat beautiful things, because our bodies are made of what we eat. No one admires brown circles around the eyes .and brown patches on the hands, and a leather- coloured skin. One knows what these things mean. Behind the leather-coloured skin is a bad breath. Behind that bad breath is impure blood—blood charged with these same offensiv. aromas that are coming out of the blood ; for that is where these offensive odours come from; the blood picks ,them up in the colon and other parts of the body and carries them to the lungs. where they are poured into the breath. The breath is bad because the whole body is bad.—Dr. Kellogg.

WOMEN'S THRIFT CONFERENCE.

A women's thrift conference, under the auspices of the Warrington Thfift Committee,' was held in the Council Chamber last week- end. Miss Broadbent presided. Miss Broadbent,' in opening the conference, said that the /conference had been called in order that the women of Warrington might con- sider what steps could be taken to spread the principles of true thrift among all classes of the community. The English nation was probably one of the least thrifty in the world, and in many an English household a careless wastefulness was allowed which would fill a French housekeeper with amazement. It was to be hoped, Miss Broadbent said, that we would learn from our brave and steadfast Ally some lessons in wise expenditure and a better knowledge of food values and careful, wholesome cookery. It was to be feared that at the present time, instead of spending less than Usual, many people were spending more. Money was being wasted on amusements, on smart clothes, and, above all, on drink. The committee had thought that instead of starting fresh organisations, it was far better to make use of those which already existed, and that the district visitors, who formed a network all over the town, would be good agents to spread the doctrines of true thrift, good management and wholesome food. One suggestion that had been made was the spread of useful litera- ture, including cheap cookery books, and another was the expansion of the scheme, already so successfully carried on at Mothers' Welcomes and elsewhere, of giving prizes for the best-cooked dishes prepared at home.

MY DEAR CHILDREN,— Next week's essay .is on "My Favourite Lesson At School," and I want you all to join in this. The prize will be a specially good one, and the closing day Monday.

_ One of my little niwes who recently won a prize has written me very nice letter indeed to say she has read it all through, and likes the story every bit as much as the beautiful cover and the print! Now you couldn't guess how much it has pleased me that a niece of mine has noticed the print; and I want to talk to you about print in books. First of all I must mention very modestly that as I have passed a great part of my long life in printing offices I can claim to take a real interest in it myself; and especially have I done so since coming to live in Warrington to write for a paper which has a very proud reputation for its fine print- ing. I know that it has, because many letters reach me from different parts of the country (and some from nephews and nieces of mine who live in other lands!) to tell me so.

Now printing is a very important subject, be- cause it has dbne a grgat deal of good in the world, and has gradualry become 'so important that it is hard to imagine what would become of us if we ever had to do without it at any time. And especially is it important to you because you all read many books, and will con- tinue (I hope) to do so'all your lives. So right at 'the outset you must learn to choose your books carefully; in this you will be guided by your parents and teachers, who will always be pleased to.tell you what books to read. Or you may 'join the Library, in which there are no bad books, although I am afraid there are many very silly ones. But it is, perhaps, quite as important that you should carefully choose well-printed books as that you should choose well-written ones; be- cause your eyes are worth more to you than your brain. Of course it is possible for some people's brains to be more valuable than their eyes; you have all heard of poor blind John Milton, I daresay. But you are not Milt Ons and ,Miltonesses, and so you should preserve your eyesight rather than develop your intellect. Many people don't do this, and so you can see the spectacle-makers earning a good living; but you know the spectacle-makers are such good people that they would be very glad if they had to shut up their shops this very day for lack of trade. Here, is a label which I would like you to paste into the book you read the most; or copy into it:— Your eyes are worth more to you than any book. Your safety and your success in life depend on your eyes; therefore take care of them. Always hold your head up when you read. Hold your book fourteen inches from your face. Be sure that the light is clear and good. Never read with the sun shining directly on the book. Let the light come from behind or over your left shoulder. Avoid books or papers printed indistinctly or in small type. Never face the light in reading. Rest your eyes by looking away from the book every few minutes. Cleanse your eyes right and morning with pure water.

These ,are all good 'stiles, and I wish you would only learn them off by heart. Do you ever read in the open-air? I used to, I am sorry to say; and now I cannot read without mT glasses. It was out on the hills that I used to go and read, a beautiful ,high hill very near the sky and overlooking the sea. What a beautiful scene! There is nothing like that in Warring- ton; though to be sure you might go on lots of

smoky roofs overlooking the gentle Mersey if you cared to. And upon the top of this hill I would He of a summer's 'afternoon with my book, in , utter peace—except for the wasps. Some day, perhaps, you will read a grand book beautiful, love such s called "Hills And The Sea," and then you will nNii7 te that is that wasif you learnvery a au cahn anti scenes. want to read great books you should read them in great surroundings, and so get the best out of them. But what I did not then realise was that I was reading with the sun shining direct on my book, and my eyesight was being weakened. So always remember that if you want to read out of doors, the best place is under a leafy tree or something like that. . div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, 1915.
STOCKTAKING.

This has been a week of stocktaking for the nation, and, like most operations of a like kind, it has provided a mixture of pleasant and of unpalatable things. We have been shown a nation so strong in the righteousness of its cause that it has given in el year 382,000 men, killed, wounded and missing, to maintain that cause, and has raised 3,000,000 men by voluntary means to fight for all that tlhey and their countrymen hold dear. So far as the country, as apart from the fighters are concerned, the end -of a year's conflict finds it in good heart. Our daily war ex- penditure has grown from £1,500,000 daily, first to £3,000,000, then to £4,000,000, and is now climbing up to £5,000,000 a day. Large sums have been advanced to our Allies, the total of them already Teaching £250,000,000, with more to follow. The workers in the main have stood loyally by their mates in the trenches, and supplies have been speeded up to such an extent ihat even in the war of mechanics, to which Mr. LLOYD GEORGE drew attention last week, we are fast making up the ground lost before we knew the gigantic nature of the call that would be made upon our resources.

Yet there are sombre patches in our other- wise satisfactory picture. Mr. LLOYD GEORGE has put his finger on the canker in the ranks of Labour. For the, most part the heart of our workers is sound. But there are some— few let as hope—who from ignorance of the real Issues at stake and the terrible risks the war has for us, persist in doing short of their
best and in trying to prevent others from

doing their best. What would be the upshot if these discontents had their way? Mr. LL9i-D GEORGE tells us. "If," he says, "we are not allowed to equip our factories and workshops with adequate labour to supply our armies, because we must not transgress regulations applicable to normal conditions; if practices are maintained which restrict the output of essential war material; if the natiorl hesitates, when the need is clear, to take the necessary steps to call fortit its manhood to defend honour and existence; if vital deci- sions are postponed until too late; if we neg- lect to make ready for all probable eventu- alities; if, in fact, we give ground for the accusation that we are slouching into dis- ster as if we, were walking along the ordin- ary paths of peace without an enemy in sight —then I can see no hope." We fancy the solid body of working men will see that dis- aster does not overtake us through the ill- conceived interference of those who do not see, or will not see, that they are playing the

div.head: enemy's game.
div.p: enemy's game.

• The enemy's game is being played in higher places. Conscription is on the witig once again, with all the risks attending a divided country. There has been, it is true, some falling off in the rate of recruiting lately, but how could it be otherwise when the authorities, from Mr. LLOYD GEORGE down- wards, have been asking for, and obtaining, munition workers before recruits? If, and when it is made clear that men are required, they will be forthcoming, and the same spirit which has brought 3,000,000 to the Colours in one year will bring further millions to fight in the same hallowed cause. At any rate, until the voluntary system has failed to pro- duce as many men as the War Office can absorb, the talk of compulsory service is premature and dangerous. When the need has arisen, and the Government say it has arisen, the country will acquiesce. What we want at the present time, however, is unity, and those who are creating distractions, either of one kind or the other, are doing the great- est disservice possible to their country and their fellows.

Ah, well! As the inexhaus- tible Mr. Carter Platte observes: Ever since, in the prehistoric days, somebody wrote ‘some- where that "The angler goeth forth in the morning full of hope, and returneth in the evening full of whisky, and the truth is not in him," the saintly pursuer of the contem- plative man's recreation has been the patient and perpetual victim of an incessant stream of wicked libels, which have by base insinua- tion and direct assertioja sought to blast for ever his reputation for inalienable attachment to the sacred truth. Now and then one meets with a spirited protest on the part of the innocent victim. Take, for instance, this ex- tract from a report of the Amateur Fisher- man's Association of Queensland "In conclusion, we are pleased to be able to say that the competing members of the Association have upheld their reputation for telling the truth in all things, but more par- ticularly with regard to the size and weight of the fish which broke their tackle or got off the hooks, and so far as our members are con- cerned it is not true that : The angler lies beside the stream. And baits his hook with gaudy flies, And lies and lies and lies and lies And lies and lies and lies .and lies." That message from " down under" will find an echo in local angling circles. •

div.head: Leather Supply Behind Demand.
div.p: Leather Supply Behind Demand.

Trade last week, writes the Warrington cor- respondent of the "Leather Trades Review," was easily maintained at usual strength, de- mand being full for most classes, and particu- larly urgent for Army lines. The supply again appears to be fallino, behind the rate of con- sumption. Ytedium bends were also active, but branded, except in heavy selections, were moderate. Home trade is good. Prices all round are very steady, and I cannot find any proof that the ease, which seemed to be ex- pected by buyers a few weeks back, has materialised at all in this district, late business having beeii easily transacted at the same prices as those which have been ruling for the last few months. There may have been occasional exceptions as regards special lots, but such cases occur at all times, and afford no indication of the state of the market as a whole. New busi- ness may be better described as steady than brisk, and is more in the nature of a renewal of expiring contracts than of original orders, though I expect that the high discounting rate on the American exchange will turn a greater number of orders on the home market, as just ' now all users of American leather are finding cost price up about 7 per cent from the cause mentioned.
