Insured Persons And Compen-
sation For Accidents.

div.head: WHY 14 DAYS ARE NEEDED TO RECOVER FROM MINOR INJURIES.
div.p: WHY 14 DAYS ARE NEEDED TO RECOVER FROM MINOR INJURIES.
Special to "The Examiner."

A matter a considerable importance was raised by Dr. Manson at the last meeting of the Insurance Committee', when he moved the following resolution:— That this committee strongly advocates such amendment of the National Insurance Act as would place upon the approved societies (or, in the case of deposit contributors, the Insur- ance Committee) the liability of paying sick- ness or disablement benefit to insured persons incapacitated from work owing to accident, in respect of which compensation may ultimately prove to be due, unless the employer shall immediately accept liability. In the event of a claim for compensation being ultimately established, the approved society (or Insur- ance Committee as the case may be) shall be entitled to recover any payments made by way of advance. That copies of this resolution be sent to the Prime Minister, the Chancellor of the Exche- quer, the Insurance Commissioners, and the

Member of Parliament for Warrington. DroManson explained that he was not speak- ing on behalf of the Panel Committee, but simply on his own account. The actual position as to liability in respect of compensation for sickness benefit in cases of accident, he said, was as follows:
(1) If an accident incapacitates a person for less than one week, the employer is not liable and sickness benefit is due from the approved society.
(2) if the kncapacity lasts more than one
week, but less than two weeks; no compensa- tion is payable by the employer for the first week, and he is only liable in respect of the second week. Sickness. benefit is payable for the first week. .
(3) If the incapacity lasts more than two
weeks, then the employer is liable from the first day of the incapacity, and the approved
_ society pays nothing, unless the amount is less than the sickness benefit, in which case the society pays the difference.

div.head: POWER OF APPROVED SOCIETIES.
div.p: POWER OF APPROVED SOCIETIES.

The important question thus raised by Dr. Manson is one affecting insured persons who are not in a position to say • whether or not they, are entitled to compensation for accidents. The National Insurb.nce Act most wisely laid down the principle that a man should not draw double benefit when laid aside by illness due to industrial accident. But it also arranged that sickness benefit should be paid when no claim for compensation could be legally made upon the employer. When the Act was passed it was also recognised that disputes would occur when, an employer's liability was in question. Power was consequently given- to the approved societies to "pay benefit by way of advance, pending the settlement of the insured person's claim for compensation or damages" (Section 11, sub-section 3). No doubt many of the approved societies are in the. habit of making advances in such in- stances. But it is clear that other approved societies do nothing of the kind. Indeed, Mr. Rowland, who seconded the motion, gave two concrete instances from his own experiences in which insured persons had been left for weeks together by _their apProved societies without benefit. In both these instances, the approved societies were eventually bound to pay, because no compensation was recoverable. But it seems a thousand pities that people who are compul- sorily insured should be thrown either upon charity or the ,Poor .Law when either compen- sation or insurance benefit is legally due. - It appears also not to be generally recognised that if ireapacity from industrial accidents lasts less than a fortnight, benefit is payable to insured persons by the approved societies.

div.head: AN UNSATISFACTORY INDUCEMENT.
div.p: AN UNSATISFACTORY INDUCEMENT.

One other point emerges which is of real im- portance, especially at the present time. Even before the Insurance Act was passed a habit of mind ,had been formed regarding. industrial accidents, and it was this : That incapacity ought to last a fortnight in order to secure full compensation from an employer. Anyone faniiliar with industrial accidents is aware that many minor accidents, from which recovery. ought to be made within a very few days, have a curious faculty for lasting just a fortnight. It is safe to say that if the law relating to compensation to workmen were altered so as to give compensation from the commencement of incapacity, there would at once be a reduction in ty period of incapacity in cases of minor injuries. Under the law as it stands at present there is every inducement to lengthen the period of incapacity due' to accident, and the approved societies save money if such incapacity lasts a fortnight Or more. Naturally doctors, whose first care is for their _patients, tend to

give them the benefit of the doubt. But from the standpoint of the community it has to be remembered that every day lost un- necessarily by a producer means so much wealth lost to society as a whole. It must not be forgotten, however, that a return to work before an injury is properly healed may be grave, not only for the individual workman, but for the community also.

div.head: NO ADDITIONAL LIABILITY UPON SOCIETIES.
div.p: NO ADDITIONAL LIABILITY UPON SOCIETIES.

At the Insurance Committee discussion to which we have referred there seems to have been some confusion of thought. Some of the representatives of the approved societies seemed to imagine that the slight change suggested would place an additional liability upon them. This would not have been so, for it is no more costly to a society to pay out, say, eight weekly sums than to hold back payments for eight weeks and then give an equal sum in one lump. But there is all the difference to the unfortu- nate person waiting for the dispute between employer and approved society to be settled. He may spend those eight weeks in the direst .poverty, which prevents quick recovery from illness.

Another objection raised was that men meet- ing with accidents would not press their claims for compensation if the approved society made an advance. But the Insurance Act makes it perfectly clear that the approved society can take action against the employer in case the injured man "unreasonably refuses or neglects to take proceedings to enforce his claim." Un- fortunately there are some approved societies quite prepared to leave their members in• the lurch to fight their own battle for compensa- tion.
The whole subject, though the resolution was not carried, was well worth ventilating in a town so deeply interested as Warrington is in industrial accidents.

div.head: NIAGNA CILUITA (1215).
div.p: NIAGNA CILUITA (1215).
A Permanent, Permeating And Salu- tary. National Document.

The year 1915 ought not to be allowed to pass without recalling the fact that it is the 700th anniversary of the Great Charter, which is, or which used to be, considered the corner-stone of our English liberties. We have all heard of Magna Charta and we all talk about it, but it is to be feared that there are very few who know anything about the Charter itself or about its provisions. It is not enough that good laws should be made; it is still more important that such laws should be executed, and that this may be done care has to be taken that they shall not be forgotten. To prevent the Great Chartei from being forgotten, it was provided in ancient times that it should be read aloud twice a year in the Cathedral Churches. Also our Sovereigns, on coming to the rone, were required to give their assent to, and make pub- lic confirmation of, .tho provisions of the Charter. There is no document or code that has had the same kind of influence upon our national life, and the effect of which has been at once so permanent and permeating and so salutary as this. It is true that from time to time efforts are made to get rid of the Charter; and it is not surprising that it should be as diffi- cult now to maintain the Charter as it was in the first instance to have it sanctioned. The duty of alertness on the part of good citizens, it is to be hoped, will forestall any danger arising from this quarter.—Holy Trinity Parish Magazine."

div.head: MAYOR HONOURED.
div.p: MAYOR HONOURED.
Druids' Acknowledgment For Delegation Services.
FRIENDLY SOCIETY OUTLOOK.

There was a fairly large attendance of Druids, local and national, with their wives, at the Lion Hotel on Saturday evening, the occasion being a tea and social held for the purpose of making formal acknowledgment of the services his Worship the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) and Mrs. Peacock rendered to the Order in Whit-week, when the annual Movable Delegation was held in Warrington. Grand Master Lavin occupied the chair and •was supported by the following grand officers: Vice-Grand Master H. Perkins, Grand Secretary J. W. Shaw, Grand Treasurer R. Verney Clay-, ton, Past Grand Master Edwin Allen, Bro. J. Bibby (Board of Management), and Bro. J. Copping (trustee), and the following local offi- cers: Bro. W. Woods, District Grand Master; Bro. A. Shaw, Deputy District Grand Master; and Bro. W. Perdue, District Treasurer. The Mayoress was also present, along with the wives of several of the Grand Officers.

div.head: GRAND MASTER AND THE VALUE OF INCENTIVE.
div.p: GRAND MASTER AND THE VALUE OF INCENTIVE.

The Grand Master said he was delighted with the honour the Warrington district had conferred upon him by asking him to preside upon an occasion that would assuredly act as an incentive to all classes of Friendly Society members to go forward with their good work. He was sure that when they found a gentleman holding -the position their worthy Mayor held, busy but not too busy to attend ceremonies like that, or to identify himself with the Friendly Society movement and its work, it would be sufficient to Make them take a greater and deeper interest in ,their own society and Friendly Societies in 'general. (Hear, hear.) He knew what example led to, for he honestly believed that had it not been for the incentive of an example he met early in his career he would never have attained the high position in the Order he now held. That incentive was the energy shown by a professional gentleman who attended as a delegate at Hanley and did not spare himself in the occupation of working for the benefit of others. That gentleman was their Grand Treasurer to-day. (Applause.) If a professional gentleman could find time to devote to furthering the interests of a society that was essentially a working man society, how much more should working men identify themselves with the movement? Efforts were never more needed than at the present time. Since the National Insurance Act came into operation they had been practically at a stand- still on the voluntary side; and when any lodge, district or society was at a standstill, as to making mew members, there was a period ahead when the whole thing would become insolvent.

"You have special circumstances against you," concluded the Grand Master, "and I ask members to make a special effort to rise to the occasion and meet those special circumstances by throwing special efforts into the cause. There is not a man here who would like to see the voluntary side of Friendly Societies die out. Such a thing would be regretted all over the country, and its effect would be felt more as time goes on. I ask the ladies, as well as the gentlemen, to join in these special efforts to maintain our voluntary side and to main- tain and pass the figures hitherto attained." Referring again to the great incentive pro- vided by such a gathering, the Grand Master said, amid 4pproving applause: "There may be some future Grand Masters of the Order here—l hope there are."

IMPORTANCE OF JUVENILE MEMBERS. Brother ,R. Perdue, proposing "The Order of Druids," said they had always had confidence in the Order because of its progressive nature. He had been connected with the Order for half a century, and he had never had reason to be sorry that he joined. They had, perhaps, made a mistake in the past for not having such social gatherings as this one oftener, and so bringing the ladies amongst them; for the ladies had a great deal to do with the success of any Order. A woman who was a good.,Druid would be a feeder of the Order, for she• would see that each child became a Druid or a DruidCs,s from birth. (Hear, hear.) Grand Secretary J. W. Shaw, responding, and referring to the confidence which Bro. Perdue said the members had in the officer S of the Order, recalled ta e fact that the officers were elected by the sa a. bers, whose fault it would be if men who con d not be trusted were placed at the head of, affairs. They were not above criticism, however, and any suggestion received at Manchester from the branches would be carefully comidered; success in fact did not, after all, depend upon the .officers at Manchester, but upon the efforts put forward in the different branches. The officers had no axes to grind and, although everybody might not see eye to eye with them, they expected to have the credit for being conscientious in their views. (Hear, hear.) He agreed, as to the im- portance of making the juvenile section as strong as possible; in these days of National Insurance the juvenile question was at the bottom of the success of the movement. Unless they got hold of the youngsters there would be little hope of getting them when they reached the age of sixteen and became insured under the Act. If mothers were encouraged to bring in their children there would be no difficulty about the success of the adult movement. Helpful criticism would assist the management in placing the Order in the forefront of Friendly Societies and enable them to compete successfully with other large organisations of a similar character.

A REAL FRIENDLY SOCIETY MAYOR. Grand Treasurer Verney Clayton, making the presentation of an illuminated address in gilt frame to the Mayor, acknowledged his inability to express adequately his admiration for his Worship; but, he explained, what they all thought of him was expressed in the beautiful language of the address, which stated:— The Order of Druids Friendly Society, established 1858.

Fifty-seventh Annual Movable Delegation, held at Warrington, May 25th-28th, 1915. To his Worship the Mayor of Warrington, Alderman Peter Peacock, J.P. We, the undersigned, on. behalf of the officers and delegates present at the fifty- seventh Annual Movable Delegation- of the Society, desire to express to you and to the Mayoress, in accordance with a special reso- lution of the delegation, our sincere thanks for your hospitality and for the very cordial, civic and personal welcome extended to us on the occasion of our visit to Warrington. We much appreciate the keen interest dis- played by you in our business proceedings during the week, an interest that, although not Unexpected from a Mayor so well-known for his enthusiasm for Friendly Society in- terests, was, on that account, all the more valued, and we shall long remember with pride our visit to a town which possessed as its .Chief Magistrate a real Friendly Society Mayor. Our sojourn in your ancient town was an

extremely enjoyable one, whilst the arrange- ments made by you-at the Patten Hall added materially to the comfort of the delegates during the time they were in session. Signed, John Lavin, Grand Master. Hy. Perkins, Vice Grand Master. Edwin Allen, Past Grand Master. R. Verney Clayton, Grand Treasurer. J. W. Shaw, Grand Secretary. Manchester, 19th July, 1915.

The presentation was not unique, for about 1898 or 1899 they made a similar presentation to Alderman Wilkes, of Darlington, who had in a similar manner encouraged their work; but he was sorry it was not a fact that they had to do it every year. He did not .say that was a reflection on the enthUsiasm of the municipali- ties they visited, but. Warrington's Mayor and Darlington's Alderman stood out more promi- nently than anything he could remember. If what Alderman Peacock had done for them was only an example of what he had done in other directions—and he MILS certain it was—then Warrington was to be congratulated upon having someone at the head of affairs who had done his duty well as a loyal citizen. (Applause.) They trusted his Worship would understand the feeling of gratitude which accompanied the gift for tho great work he did for the ()vier in
Whit-week, a feeling which was coupled with the hope that he would continue to take an active interest in Friendly Society work in the town and throughout the country. (Applause.)

div.head: SUPPORT VOLUNTARYISM.
div.p: SUPPORT VOLUNTARYISM.

The Mayor, who was received with cheers, said there was no special need for this acknow- ledgment, as he was himself a Friendly Society man, having been entered by his parents in two Societies at the age of sixteen, Societies of which he was still a benefit member. (Hear, hear.) It was one of his greatest pleasures that he had not only retained his membership of those Societies, but had joined almost every other Society. The Druids was the only Society of which he was not an honorary member or with which he was not in some way connected. (" Shameful "and laughter). He had spent his holidays for ten years attending the High Court of the Ancient Order of Foresters, and at each city the delegates had been well received and entertained, so that he had only. extended to them that hospitality which he had himself received in other places. He emphasised the need for looking after the juveniles. The volun- tary system was the best, but if they flagged it would soon be in a shipwrecked position—and they would be responsible for it.

div.head: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES MORE NECESSARY THAN EVER.
div.p: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES MORE NECESSARY THAN EVER.

Vice-Grand Master Perkins, proposing the toast of "The Warrington District," said some had declared that the days of the Friendly Society were numbered, but to his mind the position was entirely the reverse. • There was now more need of the Friendly Society than ever; with the increased cost in the price of living, the State benefits would not secure the necessaries of life, let alone those luxuries an invalid should have. The conditions of the working classes had completely changed during the last ten years owing to the speeding up that had taken place. The strain had increased and there was more necessity to provide for the day of adversity than ever before. He expected a great revival of Friendly Society activity at the end of the war, and he hoped this district would be equal to the occasion and its oppor- tutLity. They were fortunate •in having so ardent a member and business man among them as Bro. Allen. (Hear, hear.) They must take their Past Grand Master as their example, and assist him it his determination to make War- rington one of the most progressive districts in the Order. (Applause.)

div.head: PIONEER WORK.
div.p: PIONEER WORK.

District Grand Master Woods, replying, said that prior to the passing of the Workmen's Compensation Act the Druids had their com- pensation fund, and the Warrington district were also pioneers in the case of presenting a member afflicted with blindness with a street organ. They also had their convalescent fund and sent members away to recuperate; and when the National Insurance Society came along they came out quite as well as any branch in the society. One-tenth—the cream— of the Order answered the call to arms and were now scattered in many lands; and he hoped their health would be proposed before they separated. (Applause.)

div.head: OUR FIGHTERS REMEMBERED.
div.p: OUR FIGHTERS REMEMBERED.

div.head: LATE MR. JOHN WELLS.
div.p: LATE MR. JOHN WELLS.
Prominent Conservative Passes
Suddenly Away.

We record with regret the death of Mr. John Wells, which took place suddenly at his resi- dence, 33, Froghall-lane, early on Thursday evening. For nearly a fortnight Mr. Wells had been in failing health and under the care of Dr. Bowden, and the end came somewhat un- expectedly from heart failure. He died in his chair. Aged 63 years, Mr. Wells was born in War- rington, and received his education at the Heathside Schools. He then entered the employ- ment of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son—pro- ceeding to Crewe, St. Helens (where he re- mained 28 years) and eventually back to War- rington, where he has remained for the last 18 years. Thus he has served the one firm 48 years: his duties were those of head outdoor- manager, and entailed travelling. For 'three years also, he had been licensee of the Lion Hotel.
In addition he was a member of the "St. Elphin " Lodge of Freemasons.
Two sons and four daughters are left to mourn him.

A prominent Conservative, Mr. Wells was a member of the Conservative Club, and held the position of chairman of the Bowling Green Committee. At one time he himself was an enthusiastic bowler, and a member of the Arpley Club; but of recent years he had not taken so active a part in the game. He at- tended Holy Trinity' Church.

div.head: POISON GAS.
div.p: POISON GAS.
Warrington Workman's Death Through Tank-Cleaning.

Mr. Coroner Brighouse conducted an inquest at the Police Station yesterday on the body of Martin Riley, of 37,Nicholson-st., a blower in the employ of Messrs. Pochin, chemical workers, Bank Quay, who died at the Infirmary on Tuesday.

On the Monday (the evidence showed), the deceased, who was twenty-nine years of age and married, went to work in good health. He had to clean out a railway tank, and, whilst doing so, coughed a good deal when in the tank, and had repeatedly to put his head out of the manhole in order to get a breath of fresh air. It was stated that the only way of finishing off the wtork of cleaning out the tank was for a man to go Inside. _

div.head: Gassed in a Tank.
div.p: Gassed in a Tank.

Deceased, it transpired, was in the tank for about twenty minutes. Later he was seen on the firm's premises by another employe, whom he told that he felt very bad and was suffering from the effects of gases inhaled while cleaning the tank. He went home and fell on the sofa. His wife sent for Dr. Hodgkinson, who ordered him to bed. The next day he was in a very bad condition and his panel doctor ordered his removal to the Infirmary, where he died shortly before a visit by his wife. The evidence of the doctor who conducted the post-mortem examination showed that death was due to the inhalation of the poisonous fumes from the tank.
The jury, in returning a verdict of "Acci- dental death," expressed the opinion that the firm should find a way of cleaning the tanks which would not 4ecessitate the entrance of a man.

div.head: Boy's Heroism Recognised.
div.p: Boy's Heroism Recognised.

After the close of the sitting of the Borough Police Court on Monday, the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), who had presided, presented to Humphrey Corfield, the fourteen-year-old son of Walter Corfield, of 17, Grafton-street, with the Liverpool Shipwreck and Humane Society's certificate, and a postal order for 155., as an appreciation of his bravery in rescuing a little boy named Joseph Collins, aged six, of 3, Clare- street, from drowning in the Old River on July 17th. Whilst playing with some bigger boys on the bank of the river, Collins fell in the water. Corfield was on the opposite bank and he promptly ran round to the other side, and, jumping in, swam a distance of ten yards, and reached Collins. The latter had gone under the water twice, but Corfield grabbed him by the collar before he could sink a third time and brought him to the bank.—The Mayor said he hoped that in years to come Corfield would look upon the testimony as something of which to be proud, and that it would be a lesson in courage to his friends.

div.head: " TOMMY" IN CAMP.
div.p: " TOMMY" IN CAMP.
Philosophical In Hardship ;
Reverent At Prayers.
THE REV. H. OGDEN'S IMPRESSIONS.

"The truest test of a religion is its practi- cability and adaptability," said the Rev. IL Ogden the other morning to The Examiner" man, who visited the Gblboine-street minister to gather a few impressions of his month's chaplaincy, under Y.M.C.A. auspices, amongst the troops quartered on the Great Lines at Chatham.

"There was probably nothing at all wrong in the religious form of the Levite who passed the robbers' victim on the other side of the road, but there was everything wrong on the practical side. All theory must be reduced to practice. A creed is a very solid foundation for a religious faith. The man who believes pro- foundly in Heaven will have a surer grip even upon the earth. But whatever a man's creed, his real value, and the test of his power in such circumstances as are provided by a Y.M.C.A. Military Camp, lie in his practica- bility. A " Dim, Religious" Tramlight.

"On arrival at Chatham, the stranger is at once conscious that he is in a zone where the war means much. Night-time •in Warrington is garish and brightly lighted in comparison with the areas around Chatham. Dense pitch darkness is the reception that awaits the traveller arriving at night. Further reminders are forthcoming when one boards a tramcar, for a woman conductor receives the fare in a dim, religious light. About half the tram con- ductors in Chatham, Rochester and Gillingham —the three towns that make one—are in petti- coats.

div.head: Serving " Tommy " At The Bar.
div.p: Serving " Tommy " At The Bar.

' "The Y.M.C.A. has no place for a slacker; to someone of the workers falls the duty, at 5.30 in the morning, of getting tea for the mili- tary fatigue party and cleaning the tent. The evidence of military life, apart from the tents, is everywhere. The lines in the early morning swarm with men preparing and training for great events. To be within the camp after two days of rain is by no means ideal. Napoleon once said, after the Russian cam- paign, that he had discovered a fourth element, and that was mud. After a two-day downpour of rain our camp had the *appearance of a morass, and as the men assembled at the open tables for their food, and, after receiving rations in their billi cans, darted for their tents, one could not but admire ' Tommy's ' deter- mination to make the best of things. After such a luncheon. the Y.M.C.A. tent becomes a real home for them. The adjoining land is a quagmire. The tent becomes a centre of in- terest and delight. Gallons of foaming tea, served .by ecclesiastical hands, are to be had at a penny a cup. The Bishop behind the counter is nonplussed when a soldier 'asks him for a cup of tea and a four by two.' The cup of tea he understands, but the 'four by two' is a mystery. The soldier explains that it's 'one of those cakes just 'behind you,' the measurement of which is probably four inches by two. Hardly has the ecclesiastic recovered from his surprise when a soldier standing by the tobacco counter asks him for five rounds rapid.' The Bishop has told the previous customer that the Y.M.C.A. tent is not a joiners' shop, and now he is constrained to tell this 'Tommy' that the Y.M.C.A. tent is not a firing range; and 'Tommy' enlightens him as he tosses the ' brown ' on the counter and declares that he only means a penny packet of Wild Woodbines.

div.head: " Tommy's " Talent.
div.p: " Tommy's " Talent.

'` A minister without a sense of hninour, en- gaged in this work, would be shocked and lost. So, after his luncheon, ' Tommy ' foregathers in the Y.M.C.A. tent to drink his tea and join in the short social respite before continuing his training. The rival of the Y.M.C.A. tent is the wet canteen in camp, and one has listened with great sorrow to the military police as they have told the workers in the Y.M.C.A. tent that they have just had to interfere in the wet canteen, and wished that the conduct in ,the wet canteen was as sober and decorous as the conduct in the Y.M.C.A. tent. In the evening the workers of the Y.M.C.A. endeavour to interest 'Tommy.' One night stands out in my memory. The Pres- byterian minister, who came from Dublin, had arranged a draughts tournament amongst the men, and I arranged a concert. Some concep- tion of the size of the tent may be obtained when I say that the draughts competition and the concert proceeded at the same time, without any distraction to the draught players. One Was amazed to discoVer the amount of musical talent amongst the men. Pianists of first-rate order, soloists whose voices would gain them a livelihood outside, and other gifted enter- tainers, all contributed to the success of that night's gathering. The work of catering for the men brings great joy and delight, because whatever the soldier's life was in times of peace, it is now extremely arduous. After a morning of drill and an afternoon of firing, ' Tommy ' has no inclination to prepare himself to leave the camp; and in the Y.M.C.A. tent lies his one hope.

div.head: Soldier at Prayers.
div.p: The Soldier at Prayers.

"The religious service at the close of the draughts tournament and the concert will be an abiding memory. Six hundred men were in the tent. Precisely at nine o'clock the tournament and concert were closed, and the soldiers joined in singing their favourite hymns, "0 God, our help in ages past," "Jesu, lover of my soul," and "Abide with me." Then followed the read- ing from Scripture, a few word; of cheer, and the National Anthem. Finally, there was a word with the King of kings, and the solemn impression made on one's soul can never be erased. Six hundred men, just after the singing of the National Anthem, are standing at at- tention. When the word of prayer is an- nounced, every man removes his hat, and, despite the numbers, for four or five minutes there is such a silence ail grips and holds the soul. No congregation, however well-bred, could be more reverent and devout during prayers than our soldiers. "The Benediction follows. For a few minutes there is a rush on the tea-urn, the 'four by two's,' and the 'five rounds rapid's.' Then the men go their way to the small bell-tents ar- Tanged in the camp, and the workers of the Y.M.C.A. prepare at half-past nine to close their work. .

div.head: Final Fellowship.
div.p: Final Fellowship.

'"The fellowship with kindred workers of the IY.M.C.A., when the day has closed, is a fellow- ship sweet and hallowed. They represent a type of man whose religion is robust and virile. Around the supper table, sweet and holy are the evening prayers, to be followed by a banter and chaff and good fellowship, which make, a sen- sible finish to a haril day's work. No worker but loves ' Tommy ' in the camp. And all the arduous labour and ruined suits are forgotten in the reminder that in some small way one is at- tempting—and it is only attempting—to repay Tommy' for his great and noble sacrifice."

div.head: LOCAL TERRITORIAL.
div.p: A LOCAL TERRITORIAL.

In the course of his sojourn in Chatham the Rev. H. Ogden came into contact with a V.C. hero and also a local Territorial. Wounded By A Shell Whilst Digging

News has reached Mr. and Mrs. Alfred H. Tichard, of 83, Fox-street, that their son, Private John Tichard, of the Warrington Terfitorials, has been wounded while trench- digging. According to a letter written home by Private A. Booth, Private Tichard was wounded on Saturday night, September 4th. The letter ran:—

"I shall never forget the 4th September as long as I live. We went out digging a trench just behind the firing line. We had just got about two feet down when they started to shell us, and God only knows hoiv we are living to- day. J. Tichard was the only one who got hit. Watt Batler (a comrade, who resides in Mill- lane), got buried in the trench, but he is all right now."

div.head: Injuries, And How Received.
div.p: The Injuries, And How Received.

Writing from hospital on Wednesday, Sep- tember Bth, Private Tichard said : "Just a line to let you know how I got my wound. Our company were on pioneer work, digging a trench behind the firing-line, on Saturday night, Sept. 4th. We had been dig- ging for-abut an hour when all of a sudden they started to shell us. I got down in the
PRIVATE J. TICIIARD. Wounded.

trench which we were digging. The shells were bursting all over us for half an hour when I got hit in the right thigh. I dared not leave the trench until they had finished their shel- ling, which they did when or guns started to fire. I then ran quickly to another trench and got bandaged, and was carried to the field ambulance, from which I was taken to the dressing station, and here it was found that I had another wound through my calf. I have got the piece of shell which was in my thigh; it was taken out on Sunday. I arrived in England on Tuesday." _

Private Tichard is now in Manor House Hospital, Folkestone. A single man, twenty-four years of age, Private Tiehard, when a boy, attended St. Barnabas' Day School. Before the outbreak of war he was employed in the tube works of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., Ltd. He joined the Territorials in January, and went to the Front in June.

Writing to Private Lagar's parents, Company- Q.M.S. Herbert H. Bottomley, in a letter

"It's a rule out here amongst us," adds the C.Q.M.S., a man is wounded and a parcel of foodstwis arrives for him, the parcel is opened and the contents divided between his pals. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, 1915.
STORIES FROM THE TRENCHES.
LIFE IN GALLIPOLI.
" A Narrow Squeak " For
Lieutenant Miln.

, In his weekly communication written from the trenches in Gallipoli, Lieut. Gordon Man, son of Mr. G. P. Miln, Warrington. and Chester, gives some interesting particulars of what is being done out there at the present time. In a letter under date of August 26th, he says: "I was pleased to get your letters on Tues- day evening, which I read by the bright moon- light in the intervals of supervising digging and having an occasional pot at stray Turks wan- dering in the front. Fighting for the " Key."

"The country here is so rugged and moun- tainous that you would marvel that troops could have pushed as far as we have. I had a magnificent view from the fire trench of the fighting on our left near Chocolate Hill last Saturday. We saw the Indian Brigade and the New Zealanders make bayonet charge after bayonet charge and drive hundreds of Turks away. That particular engagement is still going on, and is at present the key to the situa- tion. We are at present in fire trench 800 yards from our nearest enemy, and a big valley intervenes. We patrol this valley at night, and have shots at each other occasionally. I had a narrow squeak this morning about 3 a.m. I was out about 50 yards in front of the trench while the men were digging beyond me. I was haying shots at what I guessed to be Turks in front of the trenches, when a bullet whizzed just over my head. I promptly shifted my fire position a yard or two away. One can't do any real sniping by night, however, on account ot the light, but we do ‘a little bit by day."

div.head: Church Service Prized.
div.p: Church Service Prized.
Commenting upon the duties of chaplains, he says

had a nice service last Sunday evening, very homely and unconventional, and including all denominations. The officiating minister was a Wesleyan chaplain named Clark/ Gibson, all our other chaplains having gone sick. By-the-by we had communion after our little service; and all denominations together, without thought of sect or creed or such little trivialities. I wish the Bishop of Zanzibar could have bevn there. It would have been an object lesson for him and his confreres. You can imagine what a delight it was to have the service, as we have had only three previous services since we left England over 13 weeks ago, and these, were in the form of church parades. It was a treat to see the joy on the men's faces, and to hear how they sang some of the good old hymns. Under our present conditions we think seriously about such services, and are trying to get another one next Sunday evening. It is too hot to have it by day, and everybody is tired first thing in the morning, after a night's patrolling or digging, as the case may be, so evening is the only pos- sible time. We are still without any of the parcels sent out by you, and we are longing very much to see the contents of these, although our food rations have been considerably improved of late."

Found Drowned After Over-

A coroner's jury returned a verdiqt of "Found dead at an inquiry held at Moore on Saturday into the circumstances attending the death of William Roberts, aged 35, a private in the West Lancashire Territorial section of the Royal Engineers, whose home was at 3, Robson- street, Warrington. The lower portion of the deceased's body had been found in the Bridge- water Canal at Keckwick on the Bth inst. ' Finding.of Half the Body.

Mr. E. A. White, deputy coroner, conducted the inquiry, and the first witness called was a canal banksman, named Peter Jones, of Pepper- street, Preston Brook, who stated that the pre- vious Wednesday he was told that a body was in the canal. With P.C. Collier he went to the spot indicated, and there found the lower por- tion of a man's body, on the feet of which were a pair of soldier's boots and socks, but no other clothing. It looked as if the body had been cut in twain by the propeller of a steam- boat.
P.C. J. H. Hough, of Moore, also spoke to having examined the remains. The First Inquest.

P.S. George Kingman, stationed at Bowdon, near Altrincham, gave it as his opinion that the lower portion of the body corresponded with the upper part of a man's body found at Dunham Massey on September 6th. An inquest on that part of the body was held by Mr. Coroner Yates at Altrincham, the jury return- ing a verdict of "Found drowned." The truncated body was not then identified.

div.head: Deceased's Farewell Message.
div.p: Deceased's Farewell Message.

Mrs. Annie Roberts, of 3, Robson-street.'War- rington, said that her husband enlisted in the Engineers about two months ago, and was stationed at St. Helens. She last saw him alive at 5 o'clock on the morning of Wednesday, Sep- tember Ist, when he went out of the bedroom. He had then been an absentee from his regi- ment for two days, having been due back on the Monday. He had been drinking heavily. He kissed the children, said "Good-bye ?" and went out. He had of late been very strange in his manner, and when he went out that morn- ing he left on the back kitchen table a piece of paper on which were the words, "God bless my children." Witness did not see him again. The following Tuesday an escort came to fetch him back. She identified the lower part of the body as that of part of her husband by means or a mark on the left leg, which was caused by his having been run over some time ago. The boots and socks were such as her husband wore, and a cap. found in another part of the canal, was, like his. The photograph taken of the upper portion of the body resembled her hus- band, and, in her own mind, she was quite cer- taie 'that the body was his.
To their verdict of "Found dead," the jury added a rider to the effect that there was no evidence as to the date, cause or place of death.

div.head: WIREDRAWERS PROTEST.

A general meeting was called at headquarters on Wednesday night of the members of the, Amalgamated Wiredrawers' Society to pro- test against the action of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council in refusing to entertain the appeal of Captain Mathams for their assistance during the recruiting week. The following resolution was carried : - That the action of the Trades and Labour

div.head: SLUR ON TRADE UNIONS.
div.p: A SLUR ON TRADE UNIONS.
" Beyond Bounds."
To th 4 Editor of " The Examiner."
Sir,—The following letter has been sent to the Wiredrawers' Society:— _ _ _

"To the Cammiitee of the Amalgamated Wiredrawers' Society,. Warrington District. "Gentlemen,—Na doubt you are aware of the report in. tha local newertaners of the applica- ,tidn of the officer commanding the administra- tive centmof the South Lancashire Regiment to the Secretary of the Trades and Labour Coun- cil, 'asking for the co-operation of that organisa- tion, in making the arrangements for the cam- paign for the enlistment of recruits. "Now whatever views individuals may have upon that matter does not obtain with me in the least; but we as members of the Amalga- mated Wiredrawers' Society ot Great Britain, Warrington District, and through that Society members of the Trades and Labour Council, emphatically enter our protest against the action of the E.C. of that body in ignoring such application. The least the oftcials could have done would have been to meet representa- tives of the recruiting eampaign and listen to their views as to the methods they may use. Instead, the curt reply to the application, in our opinion, casts a slur upon the Trade Unionists of the town, and particularly those belonging to that organisation. "Individuals have a perfect right to voice their own views, but for individuals to voice the opinions of a community of Trade Unionists, without consulting them upon the national crisis, is exceeding the bounds of society. EXPLANATION—THEN ACTION.

"In other towns they have Iliad the benefit of counsel and advice of Trades and Labour Coun- cils, and the Trades Union Congress, repre- sentative of three million workers of this country, passed almost a solid resolution to assist the Government in thd prosecution of the war to the end, and for a small, almost insig- nificant organisation to go in opposition to such overwhelming numbers is beyond all compre- hension.

My Society and yours, the Amalgamated Wiredrawers', WarringtQn District, being one of the first in the formation of the Trades Council, are quite justified in questioning the action of the E.C. of the Trades and Labour Council in taking such an unpatriotic course in refusing to entertain an application of so serious a nature.

"We are passing through a very grave national crisis, and we take it that we have a delegate (or should have) on the E.C. of the Trades Council. It would be wise in the first place to get an explanation from him as to their action, and then for the committee to take any course they may deem advisable. "We may say that so far as we are per- sonally concerned, and our way of looking at it, no explanation will be so patriotic as to justify their action.
'"Trusting that our committee will consider what action should be taken. " Yours in Unity. "W. BULLOCK." "77, Algernon-street."

div.head: NEUTRAL COURSE.
div.p: A NEUTRAL COURSE.

Mr. Dukes said he wanted first of all to put one matter right that had been stated wrongly. He knew of no case to which anyone could draw attention in which they had done as had been said with regard to any body. Correspondence relating to anything of the sort had first been read at the Council's meeting and instructions given to the Exdcutive to act in a certain way. Neither the U.D.C.'s, the National Service League's, nor any other body's representatives had addressed special meetings of the Council unless such meetings had been called by the Executive as the result of ,instructions given by a full Council meeting. The Executive was apparently much divided on the matter, just as the Council was. He wanted delegates to be fully alive to the fact that the question was a partisan question so far as they were concerned. They had Trade Unionist branches believing that they ought to take no action at all in regard to recruiting. They had others who thought the Council ought to take every action possible. They had the ultra-militarists and the pacifists, and between the two the Council had to decide whether to grant the request of an outside body that a special meeting of the Council should be convened to hear their views.

"IN ACCORDANCE WITH TRADITION." "We talked round it," Mr. Dukes went on. "A hundred and one questions were asked. Realising that if we favoured any side we should give offence to some other side, we decided it was our duty to remain strictly neutral. This was our view, and had the Press—again the Capitalist Press—been as eager to ask us our reasons as they were to publish the ,letters with- out our consent, a totally different aspect would have been put upon the case. It is perfectly correct for the delegates to express their dis- agreement, but the position in which the Executive were placed should be borne in mind. If we had taken sides in this matter, on which we knew the Council to be divided in opinion, we should have caused a split. We have put nothing in the way of Trade Unionists taking the platform for recruiting. We have said to them: 'lf you feel inclined to do so, answer the dictates of your conscience and go.' That is our view. I think we have acted in accord- ance with the traditions of the conduct of this Council. There has been no violation of rule, but there would have been if we had decided to act as the applicants requested.

EACH MAN MUST DECIDE FOR HIMSELF. "I am hopeful we have properly interpreted the rule by which no special meeting of the Council can be called at the request of an out- side body except by the previous instruction of the full Council. I know of no man holding a leading position on this Council who has tried to put any barrier in the way of anyone taking part in recruiting if he felt called on to do so. This campaign differs and differs widely from everything we have hitherto been called on to consider. It is of paramount importance to the workers. It is a question of life and death. My personal answer to this matter I have not put in the Press, and have no desire to put in the Press. 1 want you to realise that what was put in the Press was put in with a view to dis- crediting the workman. It was put in by those people who have never had a good word to say about you. My view is that I have never felt myself either entitled or capable of telling other men, in matters of life and death, where their duty lies. To all the men who have con- sulted me I have Said: It's your question, not mine.' I am a Trade Union official.

"If the majority of this Council." said Mr. Dukes in conclusion, "think I have done wrong, they have their remedy; I shall know where stand, and my course will be quite clear. I ask no favour; I claim I have been fair to all sections of -the Council. It was with a view to avoiding criticism by any section that I had deliberately suppressed my own individual viet, and I don't desire to force my opinions upon anyone." (Applause.) Mr. Fred Mills said he was very glad to tear Mr. Dukes' explanation, and to know that the Council were not tied down to the Executive's decision. He was also pleased to learn that the Executive was divided on the question, and that each member could choose for himself whether he took part in recruiting or not. The Chairman said that-the war was still pro- ceeding, and if the Council decided in favour of recruiting they could act accordingly. BEST COURSE THAT COULD HAVE BEEN

div.head: TAKEN.
div.p: TAKEN.

Mr. T. Hamblett (Railwaymen) expressed the opinion that the action of the Executive waa the best course that could have been taken. Mr. T. Howard (Stove-grate Workers) sup- ported. • Mr. Plinston maintained that the action of the Executive was absolutely in accordance with previous procedure. Their policy was a very righteous one.

div.head: RESOLUTION OF CONFIDENCE.
div.p: RESOLUTION OF CONFIDENCE.

The Chairman said he thought the Council should show their feelings by passing a vote of confidence in the Executive, and to place on, record their disapproval of the attitude of the Press. "They have been absolutely mean over the matter," he added. Mr. Harrison, in moving the resolution sug- gested by the Chairman, said he knew the military people had employed a man to trundle a half-ton advertisement arrangement round the town for nine hours a day, at fourpenee an hour; so he didn't see that that Council had much in common with them.

Mr. Shimmin persisted in his objection to the course taken by the Executive. Ire maintained that the Executive should have called a meet- ing of the Council immediately. Mr. Dykes reminded him that to have adopted such a course would have been to create a pre- cedent, and offered, if anyone desired that he should do so, to go and explain the situation. Mr. Shimmin said that the action of the Executive might be resented by the two-thirds of their members who had joined the Colours. The more men we got now for fighting, the sooner would the war be over, and if the matter were explained by the Secretary it would be as well. _
_ The resolution was seconded and carried without opposition.

The work of this department has gone oil. satisfactory during the past week. Friends. have come forward to adopt prisoners, and to send them parcels regularly. In Hospital.—At present there are in the Red C.ross Hospital twenty-tour wounded soldiers.
On the Bench.—At Tuesday morning's Petty Sessions the Hon. J. E. Cross presided, and there were also on the Bench Messrs. S. W. Gould, S. Davies, A. W. Callender and J. Coxon.

" Hot At Both Ends."—A Heatley soldier now serving abroad writes home that out there it is "hot at both ends—the climate and the fight- ing; so hot indeed that I have not had a wash or a shave for three weeks."

Angling Match.—At their club waters, The Pools, Statham, the members of .the Lymm Angling Society will compete in a fishing match this afternoon. After two hours a prize (value half-a-guinea) is to be given for the best specimen fish.

Scout's Funeral.—At the Oughtrington Parish Church on Thursday afternoon, in the presence of many mourners, the funeral took place of Scout Gleave, a member of the Oughtrington Troop. About 84 Scouts from Oughtrington, Heatley and Lymm attended, in charge of Scout- masters Nash, Timperley, Hatton and Farrax. At the grave the Rector (Rev, G. S. Tudor- }vans) officiated.

School Attendance.—Edward Blackburn failed to attend Tuesday's Sessions to answer a sum- mons for not having sent his son Stanley, aged nearly six, to school between May 31st and September 10th.—Mr. W. Mercer explained that the case had previously been adjourned for two months to see if there was any improvement, but the child only attended seven times, but a month of that period was holiday time. The home was 220 yards from the school, And in May Blackburn had been fined 2s. Gd. in respect of the same child.—The fine was 108.

Why There Was No Light.—At Tuesday's Ses- sions, Ernest Walker, of Salford, appeared for having failed to have a red rear light on his motor cycle whilst cycling near Lymm Bridge, Lymm.—Acting-Sergeant Griffiths stated that he found the cycle standing on the side of the road. Walker came out of a hotel, and said he ran short of carbide.—Mr. E. Powles (of Stock- port) represented defendant, and admitted a technical offence. When defendant arrived at Lymm from Manchester he discovered that the carbide receptacle had fallen away, probably owing to the jolting caused by the bad state of the road. When the sergeant came on the scene Walker had left the machine to buy a new lamp.—On payment of costs the case was dis- missed.

Private Thom as Reg an .—Private Thomas Regan, of the sth Manchesters—whose home is at Wigan—was twice wounded at the Dar., dangles, the first time in the head and next in the arm. He is now in the fighting line again, and in a letter dated August 18th to his wife—who is staying at Reddish View, Rush Green, Lymm—said they were doing very well and fairly getting the Turks into their hands. He thinks there will shortly be a great change out there, and hopes to be home by Christmas. The men go in and out of the firing line at intervals of three days. Out there he has met his brother Peter—of the Lancashire Fusiliers— and his uncle, Private Austin Connell, of another regiment; they are both in good health. "It is_like being in Heaven." adds Private Regan, "to see one of your own!" The Substituted Chassis.—There was dealt with at Tuesday's Sessions the remanded case of Schute Bros., Ltd., motor contractors, of New Bridge-street, Manchester--summoird for being the owners of a heavy motor car and failing to have registered thereon (1) the highest rate of speed; (2) the weight unladen; (3) the axle-weight on each axle.—The Secretary at- tended and, having pleaded guilty to all three charges, explained that a new chassis which was due to arrive was delayed at the contractors owing to war work. As they themselves needed their car urgently for war contracting, they at the last moment placed on it this old chassis, and informed the local taxation authorities that it should be weighed at the first oppor- tunity, the time being then arranged.—ln each of the three cases the fine was fixed at 10s.

Wedding Of Miss Hewitt.—A pretty wedding took place at the Parish Church on Wednesday afternoon, when Miss Alice Hewitt—daughter of the late Mr. Thomas and Mrs. Hewitt, of Cherry-lane--became the wife of Mr. William Dean, of Wydaile, Yorkshire. A good congre- gation attended. The bride's dress was of poplin shot with purple, and she wore a hat to match. The Rev. H. Gray officiated, and the best man was Mr. Harry Dean, of Burnley, brother of the bridegroom. Miss Annie Hewitt, sister of the bride, acted as brides- maid. 'The bride was given away by her brother, Mr. Richard Hewitt. Many costly presents were received. After a reception at the bride's home, Mr. and Mrs. Dean left for Shifnal, Salop, for the honeymoon. They will afterwards take up their residence at Wydaile, York—the bridegroom being employed at Wy- daile Hall by Mr. IL Illingworth, brother of the late Liberal Whip.

div.head: THREE SONS IN ARMY.
div.p: THREE SONS IN ARMY.

PATRIOTIC LYMM FAMILIES SUPPLY RECRUITS. Several Lymm families have supplied three recruits during the present war, it is interest- ing to recall. Notable are those of Mr. and Mrs. B. Elliott, of 'New-road; and the "Welsh Regiment" Booths, of Statham—both of whose records we published some months ago. The following are others:—

div.head: FATHER AND THREE SONS.
div.p: FATHER AND THREE SONS.

Sergeant-Major Robert Jones (of the sth Loyal North Lancashires) and Mrs. Jones— whose home is at Rush Green, have three sons serving with the Colours. The Sergeant-Major, whose age is about 50, and whose home is at Reddish View, Rush Green—is a native of Lymm, and worked as a fireman at Partington, and later at the Latch- ford Steel Works. The Army he joined nine months ago, and promotions came in rapid succession, probably on accoun of his previous military experience—for he was an old Reservist, having fought through the Boer War, in which he gained two medals. He at- tends the Parish Church.
His eldest son, Jim Hope, is aged 24 and single, and worked for Mr. Frank Thomason as a plumber. Nearly, a year ago he joined the sth Cheshire Territorials, and is now in the South.

Jack, the second, is 21 and also single. With the Lymm Territorials he was called up early in the war—relinquishing his work as a fireman at the Partington Paper Mill. As we fully reported some time ago, he had a nervous break- down at the Front, after serving six months, and now lies in King George's Military Hos- pital, London. He is making good progress, and hopes shortly to visit home. The third is Alec, whose age is 18, and who was also called up with the sth Cheshires, and who is now training in the South and doing duty as a blacksmith in the transport section. Like his brothers, he was born at Lymm, educated at Oughtrington School, and belongs to the Church of England. Alec. is an ex-member of the Lads' Club.

div.head: CLARE FAMILY.
div.p: THE CLARE FAMILY.
Three sons also of Mrs. Clare, of Booth's Hill, belong to the Army, _ _

Sergeant-Major 'Harold Clare, who is, of course, now with the Lymm Territorials in Belgium, is the eldest of the three soldier- brothers, and formerly worked as a foreman- joiner for Colonel Groves. The Volunteers he joined. some years previous to the Boer War, and was .therefore in readiness for serving in South Africa. He has now been again on active service since the war outbreak, and on the Continent since February. With his wife and daughter he lives at the Drill Hall, and is a chorister at the Parish Church.

The second is Corporal Ernest, who is aged 28, and on duty in the South as a Lymm "Terrier "—which he has been for eight years. Married nine months ago whilst in training at Northampton, his wife lives at Statham. A 'fortnight ago he visited home. In peace times he is a toolmaker for Mr. G. L. Welford at the Acme Tool Works; and he is a Primitive Methodist.

Private Joseph Clare, the third one, was also 'mobilised in August, 1914, with the Lymn: "Terriers," and served with them abroad for seven months—transferring four weeks ago to the Royal Engineers (Mining Section), along with his cousin, Private Percy Clare. Aged 23, Private Joseph was born at Lymm, where he has lived all his life, working as a labourer on the L. and N.-W. Railway. Unmarried, he at- tends the Primitive Methodist Chapel:- he is also an Altrincham footballer.

div.head: BROTHERS DRINKWATER.
div.p: THE BROTHERS DRINKWATER.
Mrs. Thomaa Drinkwater, of Dyer's-lane, Rush Green,. Lynam,- has three sons in the Army—one at the Front and the other two going out in two days. -

William Hedley, the eldest, is the one already on the Continent. Aged 36, he is married and has six children; his home is at Florence-street, off Beatrice-street, Latchford. Like both his brothers, he Was born at Lymm, and in boy- hood attended the village school. He works as a labourer for Mr. Chapel, Latchford; but enlisted about two months after the war out- break in the 4th South Lancashire Territorials. He has been abroad 14 webks.
The second, George, is aged 29, and with his wife and four children, lives at Fox Cover Cot- tages, Rush Green. Employed by Mr. Wm. Hinton, coal dealer, he joined up eleven months ago.

Thomas Edward is the third, and wds the first to enlist—in September, 1914. In the Cheshires he first enlisted, subsequently trans- ferring to his brothers' regiment. Aged 19, he is single, and works in peace times as a brick- setter's labourer—last employed by Mr. Woods. builder, of Dunham—whore he had belonged for two years.
All are connected with the Church of Eng- land.

div.head: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
div.p: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
This week a rumour gained currency that Private Henry Brookes had lost his •life at the Front. This is not so.
To his mother at Booth's Hill, ho writes: "We are going to a concert to-night [the 13th], so it will be a change. My mind has been full of Germans."

div.head: Word From Mining ,Members.
div.p: Word From Mining ,Members.

In word to Miss B. Cross, Private Percy Clare, of the Mining Section, says that Private Joseph Clare and himself are keeping well, and continues that he has received a letter that was sent to get there some time ago, but only just arrived; he got half a dozen all at once. Well, we are having some grand weather just now, only it begins to go cold at night. You say they think tho war will last another two years? Let's hope not. You know it may last for years, but it cannot last for ever."

div.head: PRIVATE J. ITIOMASON.
div.p: PRIVATE J. ITIOMASON.
Longest-Serviee Lymm Volunteer Pays
Visit Home.

Private J. Thomason has this week been pay- ing a visit home to New-road on sick leave from hospital at Sheffield. He arrived on Tuesday night, and expects to join the regiment at Ches- ter on *Tuesday. He will then be the sixth Lymm Territorial there after returning from France —although Corporal Edwin Blease and Private Arthur Hadden. may return to the Front very shortly. The Private has had seventeen years' un- broken service as Volunteer and Territorial— in fact, with the tkxception of Colonel Groves, he has the longest service record in Lynim.

div.head: WAR PRISONERS.
div.p: WAR PRISONERS.
Railway Employes Set " Adoption "
Eiample.

Efforts are being made to adopt four prisoners of war, three of whom belong to Lymm, and to send to them every fortnight a parcel of food and (probably) other requirements. The whole railway staff at Lymm have already adopted one, and offers on behalf of the remaining three are solicited at the earliest possible moment: Mr. F. E. Evans, of The Cross (lion. secretary of the Soldiers and Sailors Families' Associa- tion) will be very glad to give all particulars. To show the urgency of this appeal we may quote a letter recently received from one prisoner of war, which runs: "Dear have been informed by my chum, Private -

div.p: MB MUMMER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, 1915.

div.head: AMUSING "TOMMY."
div.p: AMUSING "TOMMY."
Popular Entertainer Visits Red Cross Hospital.

On Wednesday afternoon Mr. Leslie Harris a well-known society entertainer—came over from the Manchester Hippodrome to Lymm, at the invitation of Mr. H. S. Saville, and for upwards of an hour kept the wounded soldiers at " Brookfield " laughing with a string of witticisms delivered in his .best form. The Misses Jessie and Fanny Holt contributed violin and pianoforte solos; whilst three of the wounded themselves—Privates Murray, Mc- Kinley and Blitz—gave capital songs. The afternoon concluded, the matron (Miss Colbu,rn) moved hearty thanks to the artistes, neat speeches and acknowledgments being added by Corpofal Mitchell and Mr. Harris. Several civilian friends attended the function. In the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom on the evening of Wednesday, September 29th, will be held another concert, this time in aid of the Red Cross. Assisted by local artistes, the Savoy Concert Party, a Manchester wilt pro- vide the programme.

div.head: PRIVATE AMOS JONES.
div.p: PRIVATE AMOS JONES.

First Lymm Man Killed At Dardanelles Private Amos Jones, of the 6th Battalion South Lancashires, is the first local soldier to give his life at the Dardanelles. The news was received by his uncle, Mr. Harry Jones, at Sandy-lane, on Thursday morning in an official note from the War Office—which gave the date of his death as August 10th. Aged 23 and an orphan, Private Jones had lived all his life with his foster parents, Mr. and Mrs. Simpson, of Radley-hill, Heatley. As a boy he attended the Oughtrington School, afterwards going to work as a hamper-maker for Mr. T. H. Warburton. For a few months Previous to his enlistment he had been a labourer on the L. and N.-W. Railway. It was on September 3rd that he joined Kitchener's Army, leaving for the Dardanelles' three months since. Writing home he told how his regiment had entered the trenches 'the night of their arrival, and mentioned some "very funny" sights; it was worse than he had expected Private Jones belonged to the Oughtrington Church, being also an ex-member of the Bible Class. "He was a good lad," said one of his colleagues on the railway to "The Examiner" man yesterday, "and we are all sorry abut it. The last time he was over he put his num- ber up in the cabin and said Some day you may see that and remember I have gone down west.' But we little thought it, would came true."
Private Jones' photo appears on another page.

div.head: SAPPER JAMES OGDEN.
div.p: SAPPER JAMES OGDEN.
Wounded In Leg At Dardanelles' Salt-
Lake Battle.
GRAPHIC STORY OF LANDING.

. From Sapper James Ogden, of the 66th Field Company, Royal Engineers, the following letter was. received latit week-end by his brother, Mr. Wm. Ogden, of Rush Green August 30th, Cairo.—l have not had much time to write lately, as we have been having it a little rough. We have been amongst them, and I can tell FOU we had plenty to go at. You might have read about the new landing on the Salt Lake; it was a sight I shall never forget. We left the base on the Friday night, and got on board ship; it was about four hours' run. We had orders not to talk or strike lights; and we landed in the bay just before daybreak. All the ships were lined up, some of our Navy in front; we had to jump into small boats", as the big boats could not get in.
Stretcher Men Worked Like Blacks.

"As soon as we reached the shore the battle began. The Turks opened fire with their big guns, and with that and the rifle fire you would have thought a fly. could not live. But we kept on going, our men dropping on all sides. The first lot that jumped off our boat were blown up with a land mine, but on we went straight at them. We got them going, and by night we had gained about two miles; then we set to work to trench ourselves in readiness for next morning. The stretcher bearers worked like blacks, carrying in the wounded, all night. "It was not long before we were at it again. We kept driving them out of their trenches. both sides losing heavily. It was very hot, and we were parched- for a drop of water. But we kept the . Turks en the go. On the following Sunday we had gained about five miles, when we 'found them strongly entrenched. I had not had a wash or a shave .since we landed eight .days before. We did look a queer lot..

div.head: Very Narrow Escapes.
div.p: Very Narrow Escapes.

"I had some very narrow escapes up to then —one bullet through the rifle, two through my haversack! On the tenth day we were only about twenty yards off their trenches. We crept up at night and built a wall of sandbags, and when daylight came we gave it them hot; we were throwing hand grenades until their trench was piled up With dead. You may tell how close we were when I tell you that they were throwing lumps of rock at us! . .

We gave them something to go on with. They got me in the leg, but I can account for a few that have 'gone west.' The game is to keep the lid screwed on and not get excited, and let every shot tell. I am doing very well in hos- pital, and shall soon be fit again."
- A few hours later official information arrived to say that the Sapper had been admitted to the Nasrieh School Military Hospital, Cairo, suffering from gunshot wound in the left leg.

div.head: Served Through South African War.
div.p: Served Through South African War.

Aged 36, Sapper Ogden is a widower and has two little sons, with whom and his mother-in- law he lives in peace times at Rush Green, being employed as a bricklayer by Mr. Henry. Thomason. Last November he decided to enlist —having previously served through the South African war with the Cheshire Volunteers—and after about eight months' training he proceeded to the Dardanelles. Born in Lymm, he attended the village school and the Wesleyan Sunday school. The Army he joined as a bugler at the age of 14, his father and three brothers also belonging to the Volunteers.

div.head: LANCE-CORPORAL G. A. HEWITT.
div.p: LANCE-CORPORAL G. A. HEWITT.
Shrapnel Catches Royal Scot About Head And Face.

Another Heatley man who has been wounded is Lance-Corporal George Archie Hewitt, of liadley Hill.- In a letter from the wounded soldier himself, the news came to Miss SimPson about. a Month ago saying that he was in hos- pital in France slightly wounded. A shell burst and the shrapnel caught him about his head and face, bruising him. He was doing well, and expected soon to be all right again. The wounded, he said, were splendidly looked after witivevery care and attention—nobody could be treated better."

Lance-Corporal Hewitt, whose age is 30, is a native of Moss Side, Manchester, and came to Heatley about five years ago to work as a painter. Later he worked at the Salt Works, and had been there six months when he decided to enlist. This he did on January 2nd, joining the Royal Scots. After four months' training in the South, the regiment crossed to France, and presentl, he was put in the bomb-throw- ing section. Before being wounded, the Lance- Corporal's last letter contained a request for papers, which, he said, were "very scarce out there." He is an old Volunteer.
Lance-Corporal Hewitt's photo appears on another page.

div.head: SESSIONS SCENE.
div.p: SESSIONS SCENE.
Police Contest Ironmonger's Right To Use Footpath.
STRONG LANGUAGE.

Widespread interest was taken in a case heard at the Sessions on Tuesday, when a well- known Lymm resident appeared on a question affecting his right as a shopkeeper. Some emphatic passages were given rise to during the discysion. Harry Samuel Saville, ironmonger, of The Cross, Lymm, was summoned_ for having caused an obstruction to street passengers by placing on the footpath in front of his shop three dustbins, seven buckets, one bicycle and two bundles of canes.
For defendant, Mr. Arthur Browne (of War- rington) appeared, and said he not only denied the offence but also set up a claim of right. What The Sergeant Saw -.

Sergeant Davies stated that at 2 p.m. op Monday, August 23rd, he saw a number of articles exposed for sale outside Mr. Saville's shop. They included those named in the sum- mons, together with two stools upon which the bins stood. Thbse not only occupied the front of the slop itself, but extended in front of the shops on either side. Besides the things men- tioned there was an old bicycle. These articles extended very nearly half-way across the foot- path (which was narrow). Considering that there was an obstruction, he entered the shop to draw defendant's attention to it. Mr. Saville asked: "What do you want? Do what the devil you like! I have got friends amongst the magistrates, and it won't pay you to inter- fere with me. It has been tried on before; and the last man who tried it on was soon out of it. And I will soon get you out of it." Witness replied: "I can't argue with you," and walked away. Defendant called after him: "Come here you coward, and stand your ground." Defendant (who was seated by his solicitor) : It is not true, your Worships! Sergeant Davies went on to say that he entered the list of articles in his pocket book. De- fendant then came out with a book and said: "Come here, I have got a book as well as you." Witness did not answer, and defendant con- tinued to shout at him, and called him a skulk and a "pimp," and told him "go and get your khaki on, you skulk." He made no reply. Later on, in the course of his duty he signalled a motor car to stop, whereupon defendant interfered with him- by calling out: "What do you want to do that for in a place like this? Go where there is some work to do, you skulk." Still later he was in the middle of the road passing the shop with a constable, when de- fendant came out and accosted him with the words' "It's a pity you had not your ' corroborator ' with you when you spoke be- fore."

div.head: People Had To Leave The Path.
div.p: People Had To Leave The Path.

He (witness) had seen twelve people leave the footpath in consequence of the obstruction. The footpath formed part of the street and defendant had no right to put goods out. There was five feet width. of path, out of which the dustbins occupied more than 22 inches. Since August 23rd the same articles had been out there every day. In answer to Mr. Browne, witness said Ike did not know that goods had been put out there for sixty years. Mr. Browne: You have forgotten to tell the magistrates what you shouted to Mr. Saville. Did you get a letter • from me threatening action for slander?
The Sergeant: Yes; it is in Court. The Sergeant's Denial.

Mr. Browne: Did you shout from the middle of the road: "We are not accustomed to talk to blackguards?" The Sergeant: I did not. Mr. Browne: Do you know that ten or twelve witnesses heard you? Witness: I do not.

Mr. Browne: Was it not that whieh caused Mr. Saville to lose his temper and tell you you were a skulk? Witness: It was not. Mr. Browne: Did Mr. Saville tell you this matter had been fought out before? Witness: He did not; I have heard since. Inspector -Brewster: You have no doubt that there was an obstruction? Witness: None whatever. P.C. Gauld then gave evidence bearing out that given by Sergeant Davies. Having been recalled, Sergeant Davies denied that he called Mr. Saville a blackguard. When defendant had been abusing him for ten minutes, he replied: "I cannot talk to you; I am not a blackguard." Defendant then said at once that he (the Sergeant) had called him a blackguard, and continued: "I will have you up for libel and spend some money on you." Defendant Sets Up a Claim.

Mr. Browne: That (the officer's retort)• is an innuendo equal to slander! Continuing, the solicitor stated that when the shop had been built Mr. Saville's predecessors must have dedicated a portion to the public, subjf.-.ct to the right of putting out goods in a line with the grid in front of the shop. There was no Ties- tion about the grid or the land underneath the flag being Mr. Saville's property, because the deeds, which went back to 1847, showed the grid and the aperture in front of the shop. Mr. Saville was prepared to claim a bona fide right to put out the goods, and further to claim that the footpath was dedicated, subject to the restriction stated. The proof of this was that, goods had been put out like this, and that until 30 years ago the practice had never been inter- fered with. A similar case was then brought before the Lymm Court and the case was dis- missed, the claim to the right being upheld. /f a bona fide claim of right was now submitted, he contended that the Bench's jurisdiction was annulled, and they coulj not convict. The old bicycle mentioned did not belong to Mr. Saville, but to a boy who had left it there. . ,

Mr. Saville bore out his solicitor's statement, and said he had lived, in the house 60 years. Over -50 years ago he remembered helping his uncle to bring in goods which had been out at the front; and he had never been interrupted in the enjoyment of his right except at the time of the case mentioned by Mr. Browne. ,When Sergeant Washington came to Lymm he inquired about the matter, but he (witness) satisfied him, and no proceedings were taken. Mr. Browne (to defendant) : We will not go into this question of words between yourself and the Sergeant. Evidently you both lost your tempers. Mr. Saville said Sergeant Davies' exact words were "Shut up, go inside; I don't listen to blackguards." This was heard by. a commercial traveller and witness's daughter—both of whom would bear this out if necessary. In reply to Inspector Brewster, defendant said neither of the bicycles was his. The Shops On Either Side.

The Inspector: Do you claim the right to put things in front of other shops? Defendant: One belongs to me and I swear there was nothing projecting on any property which does not belong to me. Mr. Browne then produced the deed connected with the property and also two plans--one of which related to an arbitration mei..
The Chairman pointed out on both plans the grid was coloured differently, from the shop, showing that the grid did not belong to the property.

Inspector Brewster (continuing to cross- examine defendant): You got excited? Defendant: Yes; so did the Sergeant. —lle admitted calling the Sergeant names, but re- marked that the Sergeant did not admit call- ing him any. Inspector Brewster: If every tradesman in Lymm adopted the same attitude, do you think Lymm would be a desirable place to live in? Defendant: Not with this Sergeant here! The Inspector repeated some of his questions, whereupon defendant exclaimed: You've asked that once. You're wasting valuable time! Get 'on with something new; you've asked all this before!
Inspector Brewster: Yes, I know I have. Who Paid For The Grid?

Re-examined by Mr. Browne, defendant said his uncle paid for the present grid and for its being fixed—forty years ago. The footpath was widened by the old Local Board of Commis- sioners, whom his uncle paid, the Commissioners permitting them to continue using the grid.
Mr. Br-owne contended that there -was no physical °bat' uction, but that there was plenty of room.
