div.head: CONCERNING A LICENCE.
div.p: CONCERNING A LICENCE.
Bench Over-ride Police Objection To
Transfer.

At the Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Mrs. Jane Butterfield applied for the temporary transfer of the authority to sell intoxicants at the Nag's Head Hotel, Booth's Hill, in place of her son, who anticipated taking up a licence in Man- chester.
Answering the Clerk (Mr. Harris), Mrs. But- terfield said she had been separated from her husband (who was in the National Reserve) for fifteen months, during which time she had not keen him.

Inspector Brewster said the Acting Chief Constable instructed him strongly to oppose the application on the ground that it was very un- desirable for a married woman to hold a licence whilst her husband was living. It was not the usual practice, although it had been permitted in some cases, where the husband _ had pre- viously kept the premises, but that was only under very exceptional circumstances. Appli- cant's husband was away, and the police knew nothing whatever about him. Mrs. Butterfield's character was perfectly satisfactory; but they had no guarantee that the 'husband would not come to the house. He was a man very much addicted to drink, and probably would come back when be heard that his wife held a licence. Mrs. Butterfield: I am not afraid of that!
The Clerk: You are not going to have your husband back?

Applicant Oh, no. Inspector Brewster went on to say that the lady was granted a separation because of her husband's drunkenness. There was no guar- antee that he would not return and become a nuisance. This was the objection. There had in the county been a somewhat similar case, in which the husband returned and was concealed on the premises, and the licence-hofiler had to leave.

div.head: Bench's Views.
div.p: The Bench's Views.

The Chairman (Hon. J. E. Cross), in giving the Bench's decision, said that whilst the Bench always listened to the Chief Constable's wishes and did what they could to satisfy them, in this case they took the view that the police wanted, as it were, to boycott Mrs. Butterfield because there had been an unsatisfactory case elsewhere in the county. In the present case a lady, separated from her husband, applied for a good business; she bore an excellent character, and they saw no reason why she should not be granted the licence. She was left alone in the world, and there was no reason why she should not make an honest living. The Bench were prepared to grant the licence. Should her hus- band return, Mrs. Butterfield would have a per- fect right to apply to the police for immediate action.

div.head: POLICE OFFICERS ASSAULTED.
div.p: POLICE OFFICERS ASSAULTED.
Heavy Fines For A " Must-Retaliate "
Inhabitant.

At Tuesday's Sessions, George Moston, of Rush Green, was summoned for having on September 13th (1) been drunk and disorderly; (2) assaulted police-officer Sergeant Davies; (3) assaulted Acting-Sergeant Griffiths; and (4) damaged a cell at the Police Station to the extent of is.

Sergeant Davies stated that at about 6 p.m. on Monday ho visited the Fleece Hotel in com- pany with Acting-Sergeant Griffiths. In the smoke-room there were about twelve women and one man—Moston. The women were singing and making a bit of noise; but when they went in the noise ceased a little. The man then said: "What's the matter? What do you want? Get outside, that is your place." He (witness) told the landlord he thought the man had had enough drink, and the landlord said he would send him out. When Moston came out she waited for the police and ,said: "Now what have you got to say?" He (witness) replied "It is all over now, and nothing more need be said." Amongst much swearing defendant said: "I keep you! ,Nobody shall send me out." They decided to bring him to the Police Station as he was drunk, and each took one of his arms. As he came along he kept throwing himself about and tripping one and then the other by suddenly putting his legs between theirs. This he continued all the way to the Police Station; it was the biggest job he (wit- ness) had had since he had been a policeman!

div.head: Sprang At His Throat.
div.p: Sprang At His Throat.

They put him in a cell, and he started kick- ing the door and making a tremendous noise. As they were afraid he would damage the cell, they opened the door; when they found that ho had taken off one boot and was hammering the door with it. They asked him for vile other and he took it off quietly enough and handed both 'to them, but as they were leaving the cell he sprang out at witness's throat. They had much difficulty in getting him into the cell again, and he then asked for Dr. , who was telephoned for, and would not come. Next he asked for Dr. De Jong, who said he could do nothing, and advised him to plead guilty. At about 10.30 his wife came for him and they let him out on .bail. Upon examining the cell they found that one of the windows was broken and the frame- work damaged. He (witness) still had bruises all over his body. Thought Doctor Was There.

Defendant: You had me on my back on the floor of the cell; I thought the doctor was in. Acting-Sergeant Griffiths corronorated the Sergeant's evidence, adding that prisoker kicked most violently all the way to the Police Station:: Witness still had on his leg a mark an inch long as the result of prisoner's violence.

Defendant contended that in the smoke-room he said: "What's the matter now, Sergeant?" and the officer replied: "You have had enough, Moston." He said: "Well, if I've had enough I'll go home." As he rose to go they gave him a shove and he retaliated. The Sergeant said: "Apprehend him at once." He (defendant) did not want to be hit without retaliating a bit. Five Guineas In Fines.

The Chairman: This is a very bad ease, and you have evidently defied the law. Quite apart from 'being drunk and disorderly it is disgrace- ful to make a noise and so on. You have assaulted both policemen, and that is the sort of thing we cannot allow. On the_.first charge —that of being drunk and disorderly—You will be fined El, for each case of assault 2'2, and for damaging the cell 5.

div.p: WHO SENT THE LETTER?
Magisterial Admonition For Woman Correspondent.

Before the business was proceeded with at the Stockton Heath Petty Sessions on Tuesday morning, the Chairman (Mr. J. Hepherd) an- nounced that one of the magistrates sitting on the Bench had received a letter, which was evi- dently in a woman's handwriting. It referred to a vase which was down for hearing that morning. The sending of such a letter was most reprehensible; a thing which ought not to have been done. He trusted that his remarks that morning would be a lesson not only to the writer of this particular letter, but also to anyone else who might in future be concerned in matters before that Court. div.head: EQUINE WAR VETERAN.
div.p: EQUINE WAR VETERAN.
Potato Dealer Fined For Cruelty To A
Horse.

William Rigby, of Old-road, Ashton-in-Maker- field, pleaded not guilty at Stockton Heath ,Petty Sessions on Tuesday morning to cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state on August 6th. Inspector Dee, of the R.S.P.C.A., said that at 4 o'clock on the afternoon of the day in ques- tion he was on .duty at the potato market at London ' Bridge, Stockton Heath, when he saw a brown mare attached to a lurry. He noticed that the animal seemed very restless, and in- quired of defendant, who was in charge, "What's the matter with it?" Defendant re- plied "It's all right !" Witness, however, ex- amined the animal, and underneath the saddle on the near side of the back discovered a large suppurating wound, three inches long and about an inch and a half wide. On the saddle, ar- ranged so as to cover the wound, was a long piece of felt padding. The wound was, un- doubtedly, causing the animal great pain, and witness advised defendant to take it out of harness, which he did. Defendant said the mare was an old one; in fact, she was quite twenty years old, and had served in the South African war. "As for punishing her," Ile added, "I wouldn't punish her at any price; she's been too good a friend! I had cut a piece out of the saddle so that it would not bear upon the wound." P.C. Crompton gave evidence bearing out the Inspector's statement, and the Bench imposed .a fine of 20s.

div.head: "UNCONSCIOUSLY GUILTY."
div.p: "UNCONSCIOUSLY GUILTY."
Woes Of A Motoring Good Samaritan.

The story of how the doing of a good turn landed a motorist in for a Police Court appear- ance and a small penalty, was told at the Stock- ton Heath Petty Sessions on Tuesday, *hen the the presiding magistrate was Mr. J. Hepherd, who had as his colleagues on the Bench Messrs. G. Dakin, F. W. Monks, W. Fletcher, C. Jack- son Holmes, J. A. Ransome and Thos. Antwis. The defendant was Albert Money, of Prescot, and he was summoned for carrying a passenger on his motor cycle in such a manner that the rear • identification number-plate was obscured. —Mr. Money pleaded that he was " uncon- sciously guilty"; he couldn't see what was going on at the rear as he was driving along. The evidence of a police constable was to the effect that at 5.30 on the evening of August 20th the defendant was seen driving a motor cycle along the Tarporley-road at Stretton. At- tached to the cycle was a sidecar containing a passenger, whilst another passenger sat on the carrier, just behind the driver's seat. The coat tails of this latter passenger completely obscured the identification plate.

div.head: Result of "Doing a Good Turn."
div.p: Result of "Doing a Good Turn."

Defendant told the Bench that he was on his way to Warrington, when a strange man hailed him, and requested a lift to Warrington. Seeing that the man appeared to be quite "done up" and ill, he 'decided to play the good Samaritan and give him a ride, and accordingly- told the poor fellow to "pop up" behind. The man (lid so, and, of course, he (defendant) had not the slightest idea that his coat got in front of the plate. "This," added defendant ruefully, "is what comes of doing a good turn." Defendant was fined 2s. 6d.

div.head: SISTERS' HUSBANDS.
div.p: SISTERS' HUSBANDS.
A Dispute That Ended In The Police

The magistrates spent some considerable time at Tuesday's Petty Sessions in listening to a case of alleged assault brought by James Henry Monoghan, of Leonard-street, Stockton Heath, against Thomas Rogers, of Albert-terrace, War- rington; Mr. Arthur Browne (solicitor, of War- rington) appearing for the complainant, and Mr. Madden (barrister, instructed by Mr. T. S. Steel, of Warrington) for the defendant.

div.head: Husband and Wife's Sister.
div.p: Husband and Wife's Sister.

Outlining the case, Mr. Browne said that the complainant was a cycle mechanic, employed by the Stockton Heath Motor Company, at their premises in London-road. Some time ago plain- tiff, who had been married about two years, forbade his wife to visit her sister. On August Bank Holiday his wife called at the garage at which he was working and left the key of their house. He suspected where she was going, and, accordingly, when he knocked off work at about mid-day, he went to Sale, and there, in her parents' house, found her .and her sister. He brought his wife back. On August 16th com- plainant was not very well and decided that he would not go to his work until mid-day. When he was dressing, at about 9.30, a knock came at the door, and when he went to see who it was he found his wife's sister there.

"My House Is Not GeQd Enough FOr You," As soon as she saw complainant his sistef-, in-law said: "Oh, so my house is not good enough for you, -then?" Complainant replied that he did not want any bother and that she had better leave. With that he started to mount the stairs to his bedroom. The sister called out " Tom ! Come along !" and there- upon defendant rushed into the house, dashed upstairs, and made his way into the bedroom where the complainant was. Without a word he 14 complainant a very severe blow on the left side of the face and sent him sprawling on to the floor by the side of the bed. Complainant was a bit dazed for some time, :aid when he came round hafound that the baby had been pulled out from the middle of the bed and was lying on the floor crying. Going into the witness-box, complainant bore OTtit his advocate's story, adding that whilst he was tying, half-dazed, on the floor, he received a kick on the head, and it was that which tendei him practically unconscious. His headl.*Ws s'earcely right yet. Mr. .Madden: Didn't you strike Rogers on the chef'-.-No; I didn't hit him. I would have done if I had had a chance. I will do it some daY. if I have a 'chance!

Who " Thudded " ? The wife of the complainant said that on the morning in . queistion. her sister came to the house, caught hold of witness's husband by the hand and hit him in the eye. She then called to her husband, who ran tip' the backyard and darted upstairs after witness's husband. He must have got over the baclighte. When wit- ness managed to get upstairs- she found her husband lying. on . the floor and defendant standing at the other' side' ofr: ti 0 bed. Her husband's nioiitlt waSs Weeding' glad his face
was swollen, and, naturally, witness was much upset.

In reply to Mr. Madden, witness admitted that her sister had been very good to her. Rachel Shaw, who lives next door to the Monoghans, said that at about the time the assault was alleged to have been committed on complainant she heard "a terrible thud which shook the house and was as though it came from the bedroom of the house." Mr. Madden: You don't know who "thudded " ? (Laughter.) Witness: No, I don't. A_ Denial

For the defence Mr. Madden called Mrs. Monoglian's sifter, who said she and defendant went up to the complainant's house at about 8.30 on the Monday morning in question, or, rather, witness went into the house and the defendant stayed outside, at the corner of Fair- field-road. Witness put a certain question to her brother-in-law, and he replied "I want Tom !" Witness said "He's outside! He does not like coming in." To that complainant re- torted : "Go and bring him in. I have stopped at home from work for the purpose of seeing him." The defendant then came in and asked what he was wanted for. The complainant turned upon him and made a statement, to which defendant replied: "I'll make you prove that." With that complainant hit defendant, who fell down. Whilst he was down complain- ant kicked him on the jaw and broke one of his teeth. All this took place in the scullery and not in the bedroom. When witness and defendant got to Sale the latter-was suffering such pain from the broken tooth that he had to have the remaining portion extracted. Wit- ness made a hit at complainant, but he walked out of the house. Defendant was never up- stairs.

Defendant also denied that he went upstairs; if he had had a chance to go up he might have done. When witness said he would make com- plainant prove his words, complainant hit him on the shoulder and knocked him down, and, whilst he was on the ground, kicked him in the jaw.
Mr. Browne: Then what the complainant and his wife have said must be a whole tissue of falsehoods? Defendant: It must. The case was dismissed.

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.
FINE NEW VICARAGE
Dedicated By Bishop 01 Liverpool.

The new vicarage attached to the Church of St. Margaret and All Hallows', Orford, was dedicated by the Lord Bishop of Liverpool (the Right Rev. Dr. Chavasse) on Sunday afternoon at 3.30. The Choir walked in procession from the church to the vicarage, where a number of members of the congregation had assembled. The Bishop then formally dedicated the build- ing, the choir singing "0 God, our help in ages past." The choir and congregation then returned to the church, entering by the main entrance, the choir singing as a processional "Now thank we all our God."

A short service was then held, and was con- ducted by the Vicar, the Rev. G. Vale Owen. The Bishop delivered a short address, taking' for his text the last verse of the 121st Psalm. "The Lord shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in."

div.head: Vicarage a Memorial.
div.p: The Vicarage a Memorial.

In the course of his address his Lordship said he had taken a deep interest in the parish of Orford, and had watched the gradual growth of the Church of God therein. He had seen the completion of the church building and its con- secration, and side by side with that beautiful church a noble vicarage had now sprung up. He knew how much the parishioners had done to first of all bring, into being their church and then to complete the scheme by building a vicarage, and he was sure that they might all feel proud of the result of the efforts they had pia forth for so long. The Church's idea that the clergy house should be near the church was a fine one. Placed there was the rector, vicar, or some perpetual clergy, whose duty it was to shepherd his flock, to be their spiritual guide, intercessor and friend. The vicarage had been built to the memory of the late Mr. William Beamont, who,. he believed, started this great work in Orford. If it were true the saints in Paradise knew their doings on earth, they would be rejoicing in their work that day. A collection was taken on behalf of the vicar- age special fund.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
PATRICK'S PETULANCE.
Stranger Who Refused To Fill Up A
Form.
A stranger giving the name of Patrick Barker was charged at the Borough Court on Monday, -with failing to give information -under the Aliens :testriction Act.

P.C. Ballard said that at 11 a.m. on Sunday morning he was called to a lodging-house, 10, Town-hill, where he was informed that a man who had given the name of Patrick Barker had just left the place, after spending the night there, and had refused to give the information required by the Aliens Restriction Act. Wit- ness went after prisoner and, finding him in Buttermarket-street, asked him what he meant by not complying with the regulations of the Act. Prisoner replied that he was going to fill up no form. The prisoner was remanded on the applica- tion of the Chief Constable.
Missing Particulars Lead to Month in Gaol. ,Brought up again yesterday, prisoner said he told the deputy he would sign the form after breakfast.

The Chief Constable said that prisoner had been sentenced for stabbing a policeman. The Aliens Restriction Act was passed for the pur- pose of assisting the country, and if a man went about from place to place he had to be prepared to fill up the forms provided at each place. The deputy in this case was as con- siderate as he could possibly be. He did not trouble prisover when he came in under the influence of drink on the Saturday night, but waited till the morning. Prisoner absolutely refused to fill up the form even when tackled by the police.
-The Bench, over which the Mayor presided, sentenced prisoner to a month's imprisonment.

Warrington Man Makes 67th Court

Patrick Richard- lioran, of no fixed abode, made his Vith folice Court appearance at. the Borough Court on konday, when he was charged with being drunk and disorderly.

div.head: PINT POT EPISODE.
div.p: PINT POT EPISODE.

Prisoner Says: "Repulsive To My Finer Feelings." John Marratt, of 2,. Lomax-yard, Warrington, I was charged on remand, at ;the Borough Court on Monday, with unlawfully wounding his wife, Victoria Marratt, and a neighbour named I Mary Ann Bromley, by striking them with a pint pot on Saturday. September 4th. The Chief Constable said that he thought the case would be met by reducing the charge to one of aggravated assault. His suggestion was complied with, and pri- soner pleaded not guilty. Had To Visit Infirmary. The Chief Constable stated that the charge was first brought against prisoner on the pre- vious Monday, when one of the wounded parties was not in a fit condition to appear. The prisoner went home on Saturday, Septem- ber 4th, under the influence of drink, and made some trouble with his wife-abdut his food. Tie got her down, and the woman Bromley then came to the rescue of Mrs. Marratt, and was struck on the head by the prisoner with a pint pot. Both had to be taken to the Infirmary in a cab and have stitches inserted in their heads. Prisoner's wife had three stitches 'and the other woman four. "As Good As Gold" When Sober. Victoria Marratt said that her husband was as good as gold when he was sober, but when he got drunk she was afraid of him. It was fifteen months since he had had such a bout as that of September 4th. Prisoner: Haven't I told you to send that woman away? It's repulsive to my finer feel- ings. kSmiles.) Witness: I shan't argue with him, because he can concoct a tale as well as any man in England. ,(Laughter.) Mary Ann Bromley said that wlien she went to the rescue of prisoner's wife and was struck by prisoner with the pint pot she became smothered with blood. Cries of "Murder!" • Catherine Whelan, another neighbour, gave. evidence as to entering prisoner's house in re- sponse to his wife's screams of "Murder" and "Katie." She saw prisoner on top of his wife, with her hair inNme hand. With the help of her sister, witness pulled prisoner, away and got his wife outside. Only fifteen months ago witness "saved her life" at half-past one in the morning. P.C. Vost said that he and P.C. Macdonald arrested the prisoner on the night of the assault and he then admitted striking , the women, but in self-defence. He also stated that the woman Bromley was a lodger, adding that one woman was enough in the house. "Hell Upon Earth." Prisoner, asked what explanation he had to offer the magistrates, said he did not remember striking either of the parties. "I am a chap," he went on, "who has to get a living as best I can. I have to go from place to place. When I got home that day they ,had both had a lot Of drink and they were careless and indiffeKent whether I got anything to eat. As to this Mrs. What's-her-name, I have ordered her to leave time after time. If one says a word and I say anything against it, the other starts. It's hell upon earth at our house." Would Not Hurt A Worm. The Chief Constable said that -prisoner had been eighteen times previously convicted at that Court. His record dated back to 1872. He had been convicted, amongst other things, for assaulting his wife and for, threatening her. Unless he refrained from taking drink, there would sooner or later be a capital charge against him. "His poor wife," Mr. Nichols added, "I don't think would hurt a worm, and this other woman, I understand, doesn't take any drink." A sentence of three months' hard labour was Imposed by the Bench, which was presided over by the Mayor. His Worship was assisted by: Aldermen Smethurst, Bolton, Pierpoint and James Evans, and Messrs. W. Furness, G. Pilling and S. Wright.

div.head: LODGER AND REGISTER.
div.p: LODGER AND REGISTER.
"Aliens Restriction" Case At The Police Court.

Before Messrs. J. Rymer Young (in the chair), C. Jackson Holmes and T. Pemberton—who occupied Tuesday's Police Court Bench. div.head: MAKESHIFT LAMP.
div.p: A MAKESHIFT LAMP.
And Why It Was Not Alight When It Should Have Been.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Messrs. J. Rymer Young, W. Furness and W. Fairclough, J no. Wm. Carney, of 118, Fisher-street, Warrington, was summoned for driving a horse and cart along Winwick- road, Orford, without lighted lamps, at 10.35 on the night of September 2nd. The evidence was to the -effect that when a Constable saw the defendant driving along the road without a light he ran into the roadway and called "Stop !" The defendant, however, drove straight on. Inspector Clark, who was with the officer, thereupon jumped on his bicycle and rode after tne horse and cart, overtaking it before it had pile very fr, and ,ascertaining the defendant's name and address. The cart had neither front nor rear lights.

Defendant's story was that he got delayed on his journey, so he procured a bottle and stuck a candle into it and asked a friend to hold the makeshift "lamp." The friend, however, let the bottle drop and smashed it, and then the policeman came on the scene. The Bench imposed a fine of 20s.

div.head: NOCTURNAL ORCHARD ROBBERS.
div.p: NOCTURNAL ORCHARD ROBBERS.
How Two Youths Had To Buy Apples At Five Shillings Per Pound.

Two respectable-looking youths, said to be in regular work, were before the County Magis- trates at Warrington on Wednesday to answer summonses for having on August 27th been concerned together in stealing 4th. of apples, valued at 6d., the property of Wm. Byron, of Sankey.—Both lads admitted the offence.

P.C. Hawkins, of the Borough Police Force, said that at 2.5 a.m. on Friday, the 27th ult., he was in Priestley-street, Warrington, when he saw a number of youths apparently returning to work, being on night shift. He managed to stop two of them—the defendants. He asked them where they had been, and they answered 'For a walk." Noticing that 'their pockets were bulky he inquired why, and their reply was terse, both answering" Apples! We got 'em from an orchard at Sankey !" •

div.head: Crept Through a Hole In The Hedge.
div.p: Crept Through a Hole In The Hedge.

Another police officer said that the lads sub- sequently showed him the orchard from which the apples came, and also the hole in the hedge through which they crept in order to get at the fruit. The orchard was that of Mr. Byron.

Both youths expressed their regret, and promised never to go orchard robbing again. Inspector Clark said that this was the first offence in each case. The police had received many complaints of orchard robberies in the Sankey district. These robberies generally took place in the early hours of the morning, about the time the employes in the various works were knocking off for supper. The defendants were each fined 105.., the Chairman (Mr. J. Rymer Young) telling them that they were not boys, and that it was im- possible to overlook their offence.

div.head: AFTER SEVENTEEN YEARS.
div.p: AFTER SEVENTEEN YEARS.
Husband And Wife Separated Owing
To Cruelt

Aaron Rhodes, of 3, Rodney-street, was sum- moned by his wife, Margaret Rhodes, of 6, Rod- ney-street, at the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, for persistent cruelty. Complainant, who appeared in the witness= box with a baby in her arms, said that defend- ant came home drunk and started knocking her about because she stoppee to put the baby down when he ordered her to fetch beer for supper. They had been married seventeen years, and she had been in the Workhouse three times. Three months ago defendant threatened her with a razor. Ile pushed her hack in a chair. with the razor in his hand, and the eldest girl had to pull him off. They had four children, aged fourteen, thirteen, eleven, and one year, respectively. Asked by the Clerk what order she asked for, complainant said she did not ask that defend- ant should keep her, but only the children. She could work for herself. An order was made for 153. a week.

div.p: CAVING A FALSE NAME.
Fourteen Days For Supplying Wrong

div.head: MAN WllO STOPPED WORKS.
div.p: MAN WllO STOPPED WORKS.
Employe Of Local Firm has To Pay 110.

Robert Buckley, of 24, Phillip-streot, was sued by his employers at the Borough Court on Thursday. for damages to the amount of £lO, incurred by 'them owing to his absenting hi.n- self from work. Mr. T. S. Steel, instriicted by Messrs. Hy. Greenall and Co., appeared for the complainants. Defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. Steel said that defendant left his work at six o'clock in the morning. The firm had inquiries made as to whether they could depend upon him turning up at 5.30 that evening. He said he would be there, but did not turn up. The firm doubted whether the defendant would turn up, and arrangements were made with a furnaceman who had been there all day to help with the work till defendant came. Defendant did not arrive, and when inquiries were made at his home it was found that he had not been home since dinner-time. In consequence of his .not turning up, part of the works had to be closed down at nine o'clock that night instead of going on till six o'clock next morning. This caused a squad of twelve men to lose £5 in one night, and the firm lost altogether £10; Some few weeks ago defendant went down to Bank Quay Station in a drunken fit, and, joining some soldiers in a .train going South, went' to Lon- don. This escapade involved him in a debt of

div.head: CORNFIELD SCENE.
div.p: CORNFIELD SCENE.
Penketh . Man's Allegation Of Assault By Farmers.
RIGHT-OF-WAY QUESTION.

An unusual case of alleged assault was heard at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions on Tuesday, when James Woodward, cycle dealer, of Penketh, charged three farmers of Bold, named Thomas Whitfield, William Whitfield and William Johnson, with an assault on the 21st of 'August, at Bold: There, were cross- summonses • against Woodward ,for a,ssau4ing 'TliOinns Whitfield and doing. damage to growing_ wheat on land in the occupation of Thomas; Whitfield.

Mr. T. S. Steel, of Warrington, who appeared for Woodward, stated that on the date in ques- tion complainant, accompanied by a boy named Isaac Maines, rode on his bicycle to Bold with the object of seeing Mr. Pemberton, a farmer on the Bold estate. To get to the farm the complainant and the boy had to pass along a roadway running through Whitfield's field. At the time the three defendants were engaged in the field mowing corn, and some of the sheaves were lying lengthways on the roadway. There was, however, plenty of room to pass, and the complainant did not touch the corn. The de- fendant. William Whitfield, who was engaged in 'the field, shouted to the complainant. lie,. however, did not hear the shout, but the boy, -who had beard the -shout, jumped off his

bicycle.-- Woodward, unaware that Whitfield was calling, went riding along, when William Whitfield, running in front of him, placed the pikel in a threatening attitude, with the result that complainant either jumped or was knocked off his bicyele. The complainant was about to ask for an explanation, but before he could do' so the other. two defendants rushed up, and all, three surrounded the complainant, held him and shook him. They were very excited, and were shouting "You must go back." Johnson, who held the complainant by the collar of his coat and waistcoat,- pulled the complainant about, tore his waistcoat, threatened him, and handled him in a rough way. The defendants dragged the complainant back towards the gateway, and eventually he was able to explain that he was going to see Mr. Pemberton. The . „

_ defendants, ho-wever, said that "Mr. Pemberton did not pay the rent." Woodward threatened to go for the police, on which the defendants replied: "You can call the police." The com- plainant was greatly distressed and his clothing damaged. On the following Monday the com- plainant went with a. policeman to get the names of the defendants, when it was alleged that the complainant had ridden over 26. sheaves of corn that were lying crossways on the roadway. The complainant denied this, and pointed out that the sheaves were lying length'- ways, and that the road was quite clear, for him t&. ride over 'on his bicycle. Mr. Steel pointed out that there had never been any question raised as to the complainant's right to go this way to Mr. Pemberton's farm, but he understood that they were that morning going to claim that the complainant had no right to pass along that particular roadway. Mr. Steel contended that that defence was an after- thought and was only made an excuse for an answer for their treatment of the complainant, and asked the justices not to allow them to succeed on this ground.

div.head: "BADLY MAULED."
div.p: "BADLY MAULED."

The complainant gave evidence in support of Mr. Steel's statement, and, in cross-examina- tion by Mr. W. Hutehen, who appeared for the defendants, the complainant denied that tlfe defendants simply asked him to go back, as he had no right through the roadway. He also denied that he had walked into the corn, or that he had assaulted William Whitfield. The witness said: "I had not even a chance to speak; I was never so badly mauled in all my life before." _ _ _
---- Evidence was also given by the boy Isaac Maines.

NO RIGHT-OF-WAY CLAIM. Mr. Ilutchen, in defence, said that the de- fendants denied having assaulted the complain- ant. They simply stopped him, and told him that he had no right to go that way, 4nd quietly led him back to the gate through which he had come. The defendants claimed the right to say who should pass along• the roadway, and if the justices were satisfied that there was a bona-fide claim of right, then their jurisdiction was ousted, and consequently the complainant, could not succeed. Evidence was given by Mr. Alexander Wilson, of the firm of Messrs. Wilson and Cowie, of Liverpool, the solicitors to the Bold Hall: estate, who stated that the roadway- in question was part of the old drive from the lodge to the Bold Hall and that no one but Whitfield had a right-of-way through that particular part of the roadway. In cross-examination by Mr Steel he stated that he was only there as a witness. and .that the owners of the Bold Hall estate. were not raising any question .of title in that „case,. nor bad they requested the defendants..to do so. He admitted that there was nothing to indicate the 'part of the roadway over which , Whitfield had the right-of-way. Mr. Baker, the agent of the estate, said that no one had a right over the roadway without the permission of the directors of the company, and that Mr. Pemberton only used that part of the roadway through Whitfield' fields when taking his horses to the smithy.

div.head: NO JURISDICTION.
div.p: NO JURISDICTION.

The Magistrates' Clerk intimated that he should advise the justices that there was a question as to the title or interest in the right- of-way and that they had no power to deal with the case, even if it was proved that there had been excess of force or violence.
After coAsideration, the Chairman said : "Our jurisdiction is ousted, and we therefore have no alternative but to dismiss all the cases?'

div.head: CLE \LINESS FOR POULTRY.
div.p: CLE \LINESS FOR POULTRY.

Pure soil is a very important factor towards suless, for tainted soil is bad for fowls of all ages and under all conditions: The danger to young chickens is intensified greatly, since it stunts their growth, retards their development,. weakens their constitutions, and. makes them ready vietims to any disease that may be preva- lent. Cleanliness in the houses, feeding-troughs, and drinking vessels are all equally important. The houses should be whitewashed-regularly and systematically, neglect of 'which means the en- couragement of insect pests. The inside fur- nishings of the house, such as perches and nest- boxes, shquld be ;so constructed as to be easily moved, while the bedding, of whatever its nature, requires careful and regular attention. Special' care at this season of the year should be devoted to chicken-houses, for, excellent as many of them are, the sleeping quarters are often somewhat cramped and low. The feeding troughs and drinking vessels should be kept scrupulously clean and well scraped; 110 food should be allowed to remain in the trough longer than is necessary, since it soon becomes contaminated.7-Middlesex in "Farm and Home."
Some people go through life on the principle that the worst medicine effects the surest cure.

div.head: SISTER-IN4AW VISITOR.
div.p: SISTER-IN4AW VISITOR.
Why She Boxed Her Host's
Ears.
A GRAPPENHALL SCENE.

There was an unexpected termination to a• matrimonial case which came within the purl view of the magistrates at the Stockton Heath Petty Sessions on Tuesday morning. A young wife was seeking a separation order against her husband, and the case had lasted a matter of two hours or so, and looked like lasting at least another hour, when with one question counsel, who had been briefed for the husband, brought the wife's case to nought and secured the dis- missal of his client. Thomas Ford, tannery worker, of Thelwall View, Grappenhall, was summoned by his wife, Rose Ford, for desertion. Complainant was represented by Mr. A. Browne, while Mr. Madden, barrister, instructed by Mr. E. A. White (Messrs. H. B. White -and Sons, Of War- rington) represented defendant.

div.head: SISTER'S VISIT.
div.p: A SISTER'S VISIT.

Mr. A. Browne said that the young couple were married a few years ago. The applicant had a sister, a Mrs. Ellwood, who was the wife of the licensee of a Birmingham hotel, and being in poor health, she came to stay. • After her arrival Mrs. Ellwood had to spend a fort- night in bed, and one night as she lay awake she heard the noise of a terrible row between the defendant and his wife. She complained to the defendant next morning, telling him that he had kept her awake and that she was sur- prised at his conduct, and adding that if he did not behave himself she would stay in the house no longer. Defendant not only apologised, but .eried- and said he 'would be a different man and vould not abuse his wife again. He also asked Mrs. Ellwood to.stop Somn,days. lattr—on August 16th—he came home at 11.30 at night the worse for drink, the other members. of the household being in bed. - Husband's Ultimatum. He said to his wife "I have thoroughly made up my mind to allow you 86. a week, and your, sistdr is to go to-morrow." He then went up into the sister's bedroom. She was fast asleep and he awakened her and said, "I have come to the conclusion that I have married into a drunken family and you must clear out!" Mrs. Ellwood told him to leave the room, as he did not know what he was talking about. She added that if her husband had been there he dare not have entered her room, to which he replied that he would put her husband up the chimney. (Laughter.) As he refused to go out of the bedroom she hit him "very much as she would hit a refractory boy." He was eventually got out of the bedroom, insisting as he went that Mrs. Ellwood should clear out of the house and that his wife should also leave. Mrs. Ellwood put on her dressing gown, took the bedding and everything she had brought with her, and she, her two children, Mrs. Ford and her child, were obliged to go out at mi,lnight. They had to wait until a taxi-cab was sum- moned, and when they got into it, defendant said to his wife: "Now you are going, Rose, you are gone for good." He also said he would pay her so much a week. Mrs. Ford and the others went to her married sister's house, in Eastford-road, Stockton Heath, where they stayed the night.

The Morning After. The next morning, accompanied by complain- ant's brother-in-law, Mr. Pollard, they returned to the house to get some things Mrs. Ellwood had left. -Mr. Pollard asked defendant what all the bother was about, and he said he was determined they should go, adding that it was his intention to bring in a broker and sell up." Mr. Pollard remonstrated with him,_ but

defendant was acting like a madman, and in- sisted 'Upon them going. Mrs. Ford was turned out and went to her mother's house. The only way in which the wife could account for her husband's conduct was that "he lost himself at times," and did not know what he was doing. The defendant's offer of 10s. per week was not good enough, in view of the fact that he was getting £2 17s. 6d. per week. There was not only the wife to support, but also a ten-month- old baby-. • •
COULD NOT LIVE WITH HIM AGAIN."

Mrs. Rose Ford, the wife, went into the wit- ness box and gave evidence bearing out Mr. Browne's opening statement. The marriage took place at St. Mary Roman Catholic Church, Latchford, on January Ist, 1914. She belonged to the Church Of England, and that

fact Was the cause of some of the trouble. After the arrival of Mrs. Ellwood the husband started grumbling, saying that she was not paying enough, despite the fact that whilst she was there that lady paid an average of 30s. per week. She also found her own bed, bedding, soap, towels, port wine, &c. In answer to Mr. Madden the witness said that not for any consideration could she live with her husband again.
Mr. Madden: I put it to you that you lost your temper, and because your sister was going you said you would go too, and that your hus- band never ordered you out at all.

The Wife: No, sir. I was frightened of my husband that night because he was in such a temper. She added that when her husband came home on the Saturday following the trouble he said he had got a house and that witness could go—he told her to go and she went. Wr. Madden: Your husband is living in the same place. There's a home for you! Are you prepared to go to it? The Wife: No; I couldn't live with him again. He turned me out.

div.head: SHE BOXED HIS EARS.
div.p: SHE BOXED HIS EARS.

Mrs, Ellwood, wife of Win. John Ellwood, of the Sun hotel, Birmingham, gave corroborative evidence. She boxed his ears and he smacked her face, leaving his finger marks on her cheek. When she wanted a taxi fetched he told her to walk, and said it was only four miles to Eastford-road. It was then 11.45 at night.

Mrs. Green, the mother of the complainant, a respectable-looking old lady, denied that there was any truth in the defendanes insinua- tions that she drank all day, and that hers was a drunken family. • Alfred, Pollard,' of EaStford-road, near the Stag Bridge, said defendant was his brother-in- law, and went on to speak of the arrival at his house at 1 o'clock in the morning of the taxi- cab containing Mrs. Ford, Mrs. Ellwood and their children. Mrs. Ford was in a very dis- tressed condition. Later in the morning witness went to see the defendant, who said "I have done with the lot of the family," adding that he was going to lock the house up and fetch a broker in to sell up.

div.head: SUMMARY TERMINATION.
div.p: A SUMMARY TERMINATION.

At this juncture the Court adjourned for luncheon, and it was on the resumption that Mr. Madden sprang his surprise. He asked that Mrs. Ford might be recalled, and permission being given, put it to her whether it was not a fact that she cohabited' with her husband after the occasion on which he was supposed to have turned her out. She at once admitted that it was so, whereupon Mr. Madden submitted that his client had no case to answer. The Chairman (after consultation with his colleagues) : In face of that admission we have no alternative but to dismiss the case.

div.head: TO MY POSTMAID.
div.p: TO MY POSTMAID.

Since. that great moment when, my itearnit enslaver, You donried the brassard of the P.M.G., And first .began—no ordinary. favour— To call upon a simple Bard like me, - - I've often thought, to make your visits more, Of sending dummy screeds to my own door.

Each morn, .with bashful qualms made wan and quivery, I lurk behind my windows and await The hour (8.22) of your delivery, And when you foot it through my garden gate, However' vile the missive that you bring, You'd hardly credit how I bless the thing.

My correspondence, as perhaps you've noted, Contains no message that a maid has penned, So please infer from this that I'm devoted To you alone, and if you'd care to send A gleam of hope and comfort to a chap, My letter-box is always there. Verb sap! —" Punch."

div.head: WOMEN AS PIG FARMERS.
div.p: WOMEN AS PIG FARMERS.
WhIW Frocks And Satin Shoes Are
Useless.

There is no doubt farmers will have to ton- sider women labour with a more open mind as time goes on. It is quite possible women could do good pig farming if they could shed some of their superfluous finery and come down to The bottom of things a bit. The pictures we see of women " helping " on farms in white frocks and satin shoes won't do for pig farming. eve* on grass, although that is a very clean way of keeping pigs. In foreign countries and in our own Colonies the Governments make 'experi- ments and demonstrate to farmers different methods of dealing with farming operations, and it is a pity something of the sort is not done here. Of course, pigs kept on grass require a considerable amount of corn in some shape or other, and although there is all the makings of a slump in corn under normal con- Jlitions, yet, owing to freightage and other complications, we are not likely to get any cheap feeding stuffs this winter. It is only by utilising our own resources to their fullest ex- tent' that we can 'hope to make pig farming a profitable concern, although I think that those farmers who stick to their pigs will reap a good reward owing to shortage and enhanced prices. —Somerset farmer in "Farm and Home."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, 1915.
RECRUITING WEEK.
The Fourth Battalion Must Be Maintained.
MORE MEN NEEDED.

The vigorous recruiting campaign which had been prosecuted in Warrington and district throughout the week, under the auspices of Lord Derby and his co-workers, was brought to a close last Sunday with a musical festival in Bank Park, "which was attended by a huge crowd. The wind-up meetings were held the previous evening—one at Cornhill, where there was a large attendance, and the other, which was more or less of an impromptu character, outside the Town Hall.

The campaign was a rousing one, and it left untouched no quarter of Warrington and dis- trict that gave promise of providing men. It was excellently planned by Captain Mathams and Captain E. Pairclough, who had the valu- able 'advice and assistance of Mr. E. A. Sanders (the Liberal agent) and Mr. Herbert Hayes (the Conservative agent) in their capacity of hon. secretaries. To the two captains and to the hon. secretaries special thanks were due, but a xneed of praise has also to be accorded to the many marshals, to the gentlemen who placed motor cars at the disposal of the various speakers; to Lord Derby's Recruiting Band, and the Band of the 2nd South Lancashire Regiment, whose martial music must have fired many a young man with the desire to offer himself in the cause of his country; and to the Liverpool Scottish Pipers, whose rousing reels and strathspeys were of great service in gathering the crowds together to hear the spoken appeals. Another party to whom thanks are due is the Clerk of the Weather, who throughout the campaigning week was in one of his cheeriest moods—considering the time of the.year—and did not send as much as a spot 9f rain to mar the meetings.

div.head: LARGE CROWD LISTENS TO THE CALL ON CORNH ILL.
div.p: LARGE CROWD LISTENS TO THE CALL ON CORNH ILL.

The crowd at Saturday night's meeting on Cornhill was a bumper one, and it was as enthusiastic as it was large. Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., C.V.0., presided, and accom- panying him was Lady Greenall, others present including: Major Monks, 'Captains Henshall and B. S. Townroe, Sergeant R. Done, Alderman Smethurst, and Messrs. F. L. Joseph (Liver- pool), Sam Thompson (Llangollen, Unionist candidate, for Merionethshire), E. A. White, J. Fulton-Smith, Charles Plinston, J. McDermid, G. Wilson, Herbert Hayes, and Walter Ashton.

div.head: SIR GILBERT GREENALL AND
div.p: SIR GILBERT GREENALL AND
VOLUNTARY SYSTEM. "The Pride and Boast of the Country For Years."

Sir Gilbert Greensll began by congratulating those responsible for the organising of the campaign and hoped that their efforts would bear immediate fruit. The powerful speeches which had been made during the past few days surely could not have failed to bring home to all men of military age the very important duty that was before them in the terrible crisis through which the country was now passing. It would be lamentable if the volun- tary system, which had been the pride and boast of this country for many years, was to break down at such a time as this. (Applause.) It was entirely in the hands of the young and able-bodied men to say whether that system was to prove the success they had always said it would prove. (Hear, hear.) There was little doubt in the minds of thinking men that it would prove to be the right thing in the end. (Applause.)

Mr. F. L. Joseph also began with a tribute of praise to those responsible for the arrangements and added a word of thanks to the Mayor, who, he said, had thrown himself heart and soul into the work. The town of Warrington, he went on, had done finely in sending so many men to the colours, but more were still wanted, not only from that good old town, but from every other town throughout the length and breadth of the country. Mr. Sam Thompson said the only way to prevent the Germans invading England was to defeat them where they were—to drive them back into their own country and to smash them there. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: LADY GREENALL'S APPEAL.
div.p: LADY GREENALL'S APPEAL.

Lady Greenall, who was warmly applauded, proposed a vote of thanks to the speakers and appealed to the women of Warrington to do all they could to give assistance in the present troubloUs times. Let them give their hus- bands, their brothers, with a brave heart; let them send them forth heartened by the know- ledge that their womenfolk—their wives and mothers and sisters—were waiting and watch- ing for their return, so that they could receive them as gallant heroes who had nobly done their duty. (Applause.)
SHALL THE BATTALION BE MERGED?

Major Monks, in seconding the vote of thanks, made a strong appeal for more men and went on to refer in terms of eulogy to the services of the Ist, 2nd and 3rd Battalions. During the month of May, he said, the Ist Battalion had only four days out df the trenches because there were no other men to take their places, and if recruits could not be obtained for the 4th Battalion it would have to be amalgamated with another. Certainly a battalion which has been given the name by its Brigadier of "The Unbreakable 4th" deserved to continue throughout the war. • (Hear, hear.) In Weeton Camp there was the Third 4th Battalion. The strength should be about 800. About 250 had been taken from them, and at the present time the strength was about 150. Need he say more?
The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried with cheers, after which Sir Gil- bert Greenall was accorded a similar compli- ment for presiding.
Cheers for the 4i'h South Lancashires brought the meeting—the biggest rally of the campaign —to a close.

After the meeting a torchlight procession, including the Warrington Training Corps, the Church Lads' Brigade, and the Boy Scouts, wended its way to the Town Hall, where Capt. Mathams briefly addressed the crowd, thank- ing the Mayor and Corporation, the municipal officials, the political agents and others for their help in the campaign. The meeting concluded with cheers for the men at the Front and for Sir Gilbert Greenall. MUSICAL FESTIVAL.

div.head: RUNCORN STATIONMASTER KILLED.
div.p: RUNCORN STATIONMASTER KILLED.
Knocked Down By Express.

Mr. James Bryden, the Runcorn station- master, was taken to the Cottage Hospital on Wednesday suffering from injuries to the head and back, sustained through being knocked down by a London express shortly after six o'clock.
Mr. Bryden went down the line to 'superin- tend the shunting of two coaches from the Northwich train, and it was while so doing that the a.ocident occurred.

He was pickid up in the permanent way in an unconscious condition, but after receiving attention from Drs. M'Lennan and M'Donnell, who were summoned immediately, lie recovered consciousness, and was conveyed to the hos- pital. A few hours after admission, however, he succumbed. Deceased had been in the service of the London and North-Western Railway a long period. Prior to taking up duties at Run- corn he was for a number of years stationmaster at Wavertree.

A Brave Man.—Peter Littler, of 80, Parr Stock-road, was honoured at St. Helens Police Court on Saturday by the presentation of the Royal Humane Society's medal and certificate fir attempting to save the life of a boy. The Chief Constable said that Littler had already received a silver medal and certificate from the Liverpool Shipwreck and Humane Society for having in September, 1908, descended into a well at Baxter's chemical works and rescued two men who had been overcome by poisonous fumes. In July last a boy of nine, named Thomas Spencer, of 121, Chancery-lane, fell into the reservoir at Baxter's works. The pool was very deep, and the water strongly impregnated with chemical waste, but Littler endeavoured until he became exhausted to find the boy. He was, however, compelled to give up. div.head: WAR-TIME MAXIMS.
div.p: WAR-TIME MAXIMS.
For Men.
If fit, enlist: this is the highest servico you can

render. One and all, get to work, and keep at work. Do your own job as well as you can. Change it, if you are more wanted elsewhere. Do two men's work, to set free the other man. Use your spare time for training or service. Don't employ needless labour. Don't grumble. _

For Women. Keep no one back: urge your men to go. Rouse all to do their best. Keep the home pure and bright. See that your children obey you. Guard the girls and guide the boys. Take care that the house is clean and healthy. Banish flies, and dirt, and smells. Use more vegetables: grow them if you can. Throw nothing away. Set some man free to light, hi doing his work. Give all the help you can, by nursing, needle- work, visiting, &c. Keep on writing to the men at the Front.

About Money. Live very simply: be economical all round. Burn less coal and gas: stay at home more. Spend no more than is necessary. Have no debts, but pay ready money. Shop early, and carry your own parcels. Give to the War Relief Funds. Keep on giving to God's work at home and abroad. Save all you can: hard times are coming.
For Young People. Serve your country by learning to work well. Be useful, not troublesome; helpful not mis-
chievous. Obey orders, as the soldiers do. Follow now, that later you may wisely lead. Girls, be quiet, sensible and self-controlled; not
flighty and foolish. Boys and lads, play the man. Learn to drill and shoot.
God And The War.
Remember God: "He sitteth in the throne judging right 7 Read your Bible, and try to see God's hand in events; and, where you cannot see, stilt trust. Pray morning, noon, and night, for Yourself and
' others. - Pray for courage, perseverance, vidory, Hold fast faith in God, hope for the world, and

charity 'towards all. Go on without flinching till the end is won. Bear inconvenience and privation cheerfully. Accept sorrow and suffering with fortitude. See to it that our dead shall not have died in
vain. Learn from their deaths to value more the dying
love of Christ. Help to purge England of the sins that are Fer weakness and disgrace. Live worthily of the England for which her sons
are paying the price- of blood. —Leaflet issued by Lee and Nightingale, Liverpool.

CHRIST CHURCH SCHOOL SERMONS.
Visit Of Lord Bishop 01 Liverpool.

The annual day and Sunday school sermons were preached in Christ Church, Padgate, on Sunday, the morning preacher being the Rev. S. E. Dymott (vicar of Glazebury), and the evening preacher the Lord Bishop of Liverpool (the Rt. Rev. Dr. Chavasse).

Preaching from Nehemiah's well-known words "Remember God, and fight," the Bishop said that in this war the nien of England were fighting for their homes, wives and children against a nation which was aiming at world- wide power. They were also fighting for honour, for the nation • had pledged its word to respect, maintain and defend the neutrality of Belgium. More even that that, they were fight' ing for the liberty of the world against the arrogant German bid for universal supremacy.
If The Germans Won -!

If the Germans won their methods would pre. • vail, and those methods were such as nobody in Britain desired. Above all, this country was fighting for Christian ideals and Christian truths. The country was also fighting for faith and morals against a foe who had proved itself utterly dead to principles of humanity or morality. He was afraid that the masses of English people did not realise the gravity of the situation. They were fighting a military nation who had been making huge preparations for over 40 years. They were organised in a man- ner which excited our admiration. The Ger- mans realised that they were fighting for their very existence, and were putting all their energy into the fight. Was this country doing: the same? They expected a great advance in Flanders last spring, but although they had' consolidated and strengthened their lines, they were in the same place as they were eight months ago. What were they to do? Take the words of Nehemiah as their motto, "Remember God, and fight!"

div.head: SUICIDE.
div.p: SUICIDE.
Warrington Filecutter In Paddington Locks.

At the Stocks Inn, Padgate, on Friday, be- fore Mr. Brighouse, an inquest was held on the' body of John Kenwright, of Padgate. John Edward Kenwright identified the body as that of his father, who had been a file- cutter for forty years, and was in the employ of Messrs. Stubs, of Warrington. He lost his wife about twelve months ago, and had latterlY been living in Green-lane, Padgate, with his brother. He had been away from work for the last five weeks, suffering from nervous debilitr; indeed, he had not been in good health for some time since. When the witness got up at 6.30 on Wednesday morning he looked into his father's room but found that he was not there. However, he attached no importance to the fact as his father was in the habit of going for early morning walks. A few hours later his father's body was brought home in a cart. Peter Rathbone, lock-keeper at Paddington* said that at 5.30 on Wednesday morning be found a -cap and jacket, belonging to the deceased, on the canal bank. Attached to the cap was a piece of cardboard bearing the name "John Kenwright." P.C. Edelsten spoke to recovering the bodi. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide. whilst of unsound mind."
